bio.en: Dan Hockenmaier is VP of Growth at Faire, a B2B marketplace for independent retailers, where he owns growth modeling and marketplace strategy; before Faire he led growth at Thumbtack and founded Basis One, a consultancy that built growth models for 20-30 startups.
bio.zh: Dan Hockenmaier 是 Faire 的增长副总裁。Faire 是一个面向独立零售商的 B2B 市场，他在那里负责增长建模与市场策略；加入 Faire 之前，他在 Thumbtack 领导增长，并创立了 Basis One——一家为二三十家创业公司搭建增长模型的咨询公司。

summary.en: A growth model breaks a business down into a few building blocks — acquisition, retention, and monetization for SaaS, plus transaction volume and order value for marketplaces — and the biggest, most under-appreciated lever is almost always retention, especially the very first user experience. Building the model yourself from first principles is the point (templates help little), and the payoff is a common currency to allocate resources across teams during planning. For marketplaces, demand is the only thing that truly matters: liquidity is the first metric to nail, share of wallet measures depth over breadth, and you should acquire supply only insofar as it improves the customer experience. The future of marketplaces trends toward higher commissions for more value-chain work, with businesses that need supplier creativity (Etsy, Faire) staying marketplaces while commoditized ones (ride-sharing) consolidate into owned-supply models.
summary.zh: 增长模型把一个生意拆成几个积木块——SaaS 是获客、留存、变现，市场类再加上交易量和客单价——而最大、最被低估的杠杆几乎永远是留存，尤其是第一次用户体验。从第一性原理自己把模型搭出来才是关键（模板帮助不大），回报是能在规划时给跨团队资源分配提供一把通用货币。对市场来说，需求才是唯一真正要紧的：流动性是第一个要搞定的指标，钱包份额衡量的是深度而非广度，而且你只在『它能改善客户体验』的范围内去获取供给。市场的未来趋势是：为价值链里更多的工作收更高佣金；需要供给方创意的生意（Etsy、Faire）会留在市场模式，而商品化的（打车）会整合进自有供给模型。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: One lesson I learned the hard way a bunch of times on this is that if you think about running a marketplace, you're basically like a gardener. You have to have a very light touch. If you're building a SaaS business, you're a construction worker, you're building the product and the features and selling it, and it's this very linear thing. For a marketplace, you're like messing with this ecosystem that you don't actually really understand how it works. And sometimes you might do something over here which drives this long-term effect two months later, and then you're going to be pulling your hair out two months later trying to figure out what you did over here that made that thing happen. So I think that the main advice is like to tread lightly. When you're messing with the core incentives or mechanisms of a marketplace, be very careful, particularly if you've got something that's working on playing with those variables.
turns.zh: 我在这个上吃了很多亏、学到的一个教训是：如果你想想运营一个市场，你基本像个园丁。你得有非常轻的触感。如果你在建 SaaS 生意，你是个建筑工，你在建产品和功能、卖它，那是个非常线性的事。对市场，你像在捣鼓这个你其实不太懂它怎么运作的生态系统。有时你在这边做点啥，两个月后驱动一个长期效应，然后你两个月后抓狂试图搞清楚你在这边做了啥导致那边发生。所以我觉得主要建议是轻手轻脚。当你在动一个市场的核心激励或机制，要非常小心，尤其如果你有某些东西在运作、还在玩那些变量。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Welcome to Lenny's podcast. I'm Lenny and my goal here is to help you get better at the craft of building and growing products. turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier

turns.en: I'm excited to chat with my friend, John Cutler, from Podcast Sponsor Amplitude. Hey John.

turns.en: Hey, Ashley, head of marketing and flat file. How many B2B SaaS companies would you estimate need to import CSV files from their customers?
turns.zh: 嘿，Ashley，市场和 flat file 的负责人。你会估多少 B2B SaaS 公司需要从他们客户导入 CSV 文件？

turns.zh: 而他们多少搞砸那个、以及搞砸时发生什么？

turns.zh: 嗯，基于我们数据，大概三分之一的人会考虑换另一家公司，只因 onboarding 一次坏体验。所以如果你的 CSV 导入器不工作，而那超常见——考虑到客户文件满是意外数据和格式——他们会走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am 0% surprised to hear that. I've consistently seen that improving onboarding is one of the highest leverage opportunities for both signup conversion and increasing long-term retention. Getting people to your aha moment more quickly and reliably is so incredibly important.
turns.zh: 我 0% 惊讶听到那个。我一贯看到改善 onboarding 是最高杠杆机会之一，既为注册转化又为增加长期留存。让人们更快更可靠地到你的 aha 时刻，极其重要。

turns.en: Totally. It's incredible to see how our customers like Square, Spotify and Zuora are able to grow their businesses on top of flat file, this because flawless data onboarding acts like a catalyst to get them and their customers where they need to go faster.
turns.zh: 完全。看到我们客户像 Square、Spotify、Zuora 能在 flat file 上增长他们的生意，不可思议，因为这因为无缝数据 onboarding 像个催化剂让他们和他们客户更快到他们需要去的地方。

turns.en: If you'd like to learn more or get started, check out Flatfile at flatfile.com/lenny.
turns.zh: 如果你想学更多或开始，去 flatfile.com/lenny 看 Flatfile。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Dan Hockenmaier, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Dan Hockenmaier，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: It's great to be here.
turns.zh: 很高兴在这。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's great to have you here. So we are actual real life friends and we've collaborated on a number of writing projects, including the race car growth framework and a whole thing on consumer growth strategy. But there's a couple topics that we've never actually dug deep into and that you haven't written about. So I'm really excited to dig into two specific things in our chat today.
turns.zh: 你在这真棒。所以我们是真实生活的朋友、我们合作过一些写作项目，包括赛车增长框架和整个消费增长战略的东西。但有 couple 话题我们从不真深挖、而你从没写过。所以我真兴奋深挖两个具体事在我们的聊天今天。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is growth models and two is just marketplace growth strategy and all things around marketplace growth. But before we get into all that, can you just give us a 55 second background on all of the wonderful things that you've done in your career?
turns.zh: 一是增长模型、二是就市场增长战略和围绕市场增长的一切。但在我们进所有那之前，你能就给我们个 55 秒背景关于所有你职业生涯做的奇妙事吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So I feel very fortunate being able to work on a bunch of consumer and marketplace businesses for a long time. I started in consulting at BCG and then in private equity. I don't think I learned much about how to actually run a business at those places, but I did learn a lot about how to think about them. I think my real education on this began at Thumbtack. So I joined when there were about 30 people and we just had to figure it out. I was there for a little over three years and we more than 10Xed the business in that time.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。所以我感到非常幸运能工作在一堆消费和市场生意很久。我在 BCG 咨询起步、然后在私募。我觉得我在那些地方没学到多少怎么真运营生意，但我确实学到很多怎么想它们。我觉得我在这上的真教育始于 Thumbtack。所以我加入时大概 30 人、我们就是得搞明白。我在那三年多、我们那期间 10 倍多生意。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: From there I built a strategy consulting firm where we worked with a bunch of the top gross stage marketplaces on a range of topics, and ultimately that firm was acquired by Faire where I am today. So I lead the strategy analytics team at Faire. I think this is probably the most fun I've ever had in my career. It's just the incredible mix of the team. The business is really strong and I love the customers we're serving. So it's a marketplace connecting local retailers and independent brands, and I just think that's a really fun group of customers to build for.
turns.zh: 从那我建了个战略咨询公司，我们跟一堆顶级成长阶段市场合作过一系列话题，最终那公司被 Faire 收购——我今天的所在。所以我在 Faire 领导战略分析团队。我觉得这可能是我职业生涯最有趣过。只是团队不可思议的组合。生意真强、我爱我们服务的客户。所以它是个连接本地零售商和独立品牌的市场，而我觉得那是群真有趣的客户去建给。

turns.speaker: Lenn
turns.en: Awesome. And we're going to chat a bit about the stuff that you do there and marketplaces. But before we get into marketplaces, I wanted to start with our first topic, which is around growth models. So people may have heard this term, this general idea. Just to set the stage, can you just describe what is a growth model and why is it useful to think about your business through the lens of a growth model?
turns.zh: 太棒。而我们会聊点你在那做的和市场的事。但在我们进市场之前，我想从我们第一个话题开始，关于增长模型。所以人们可能听过这术语、这一般想法。就铺舞台，你能就描述什么是增长模型、以及为什么通过增长模型的透镜想你的生意有用？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So I think it's useful in many contexts. If I apply it to the current work that I'm doing, the strategy analytics team at Faire does a bunch of work to help our other teams make better decisions. So we're typically diving really deep into a bunch of topics across the business. I think it's really easy to make that work kind of go off the rails or go too deep unless you have a conceptual understanding of how the whole business that it comes together. And that's how I think about a growth model, so the analytical representation of how the business grows and it's typically built in a spreadsheet which has a really nice feature of being very hard to fake. You can talk about a business conceptually, but when you actually have to get it to line up and link in a model, it's very hard to not force yourself to understand how the business works. So I think it's very valuable for that.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得在很多语境有用。如果我把应用到我当前工作，Faire 的战略分析团队做一堆工作帮我们其他团队做更好决定。所以我们通常深挖跨生意的一堆话题。我觉得那工作很容易脱轨或钻太深，除非你对整个生意怎么拼在一起有个概念理解。而那是我想增长模型的方式，所以是对生意怎么增长的解析表达、它通常建在 spreadsheet 里、有个真 nice 特性是很难造假。你能概念聊一个生意，但当你真得让它对齐、在模型里连起来，很难不逼自己懂生意怎么运作。所以我觉得那极有价值为那个。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I think 50% of the value you get from it is simply building the model. It forces you to understand it and then you get this artifact which you can use to understand how to weigh different opportunities or understand the benefit of working on different things. I think importantly it is not a forecasting tool, so it's not going to replace what your finance team is building to project the business. In fact, often the output can be highly variable because you're playing with lots of these assumptions, but it is a great tool for kind of opportunity assessment for the business.
turns.zh: 我觉得你从它得的价值 50% 就只是建模型。它逼你懂它、然后你得这个工件能用它懂怎么权衡不同机会或懂做不同事的收益。我觉得重要地它不是个预测工具，所以它不会替你财务团队建的投影生意。事实上，输出常高度可变因为你在玩很多这些假设，但它是个好工具为机会评估为生意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So maybe a simple way to think about it, just summarizing, is it's essentially a formula for your business that often lives in Excel that kind of summarizes and puts together all the things that can drive your business. Is that a simple way [inaudible 00:07:19]?
turns.zh: 太棒。所以也许简单方式想它，就总结，是它本质是你生意的一个公式、常住在 Excel 里、那种总结并把所有能驱动你生意的东西放一起。那是简单方式[听不清 00:07:19]？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah. That's exactly right.
turns.zh: 对。那完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. So we're going to go through examples of these growth models and how you've thought about this in actual potential formulas for companies. But first, just broadly, how would someone approach figuring this out for themselves? How would you build a growth model for your own business?
turns.zh: 甜。所以我们要走过这些增长模型的例子、和你怎么想这个在实际潜在公式为公司。但首先， broadly，有人会怎么接近搞清这个为他们自己？你会怎么为你自己生意建个增长模型？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So if you think about some of the basic building blocks and probably the simplest use case would be a SaaS business, there's really three components that you need to build for that. One is to understand your acquisition channels. Are you looking at paid marketing or sales or viral kind of customer referrals? And for each of those you have some different assumptions around traffic or spend or conversion rate, those kind of things. So that's the first section. Second would be retention. So at what rate are these customers activating? And then have some kind of basic monthly retention curve. So how long are they staying around? What's the survival rate in each of these? And those kind of stack over time. And then you have monetization. So in the simplest example, they might be paying you some monthly or annual fee and so that translates in monetization.
turns.zh: 所以如果你想想一些基本构建块、大概最简单用例会是个 SaaS 生意，有真三个组件你需要建为那个。一是懂你的获取渠道。你看付费营销或销售或病毒式客户推荐？而对每个你有不同假设关于流量或花费或转化率，那种东西。所以那是第一部分。第二会是留存。所以这些客户以啥率激活？然后有些基本月度留存曲线。所以他们留多久？每个的存活率是多少？而那些随时间堆叠。然后你有变现。所以在最简单例子，他们可能付你些月度或年度费、那转成变现。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So actually if you're modeling a relatively simple SaaS business, those are the only core building blocks you need and you add a lot more complexity on it based on your kind of individual business that you're building. If you then are trying to build this for more of a transactional business, you need to layer on the way that your current kind of retained customers start to transact. So how many transactions per month? What's the AOV? And then you're also going to typically need to build unit economics because those businesses often have higher costs. And so you're going to be thinking about cogs or other major costs that you build into it.
turns.zh: 所以其实如果你在建模相对简单 SaaS 生意，那些是你唯一需要的核心构建块、你加很多更多复杂基于你建的个体生意。如果你然后试图为更多交易型生意建这个，你需要叠加上你当前留存客户开始交易的方式。所以每月多少交易？AOV 多少？然后你通常也需要建单位经济因为那些生意常更高成本。所以你要想 cogs 或其他主要成本你建进它。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And then one click beyond that would be to build this for marketplace business. So now what we've talked about is mostly modeling like the demand side of a business. So now you'd also need to think about supply acquisition and retention and how these two sides interact. So as we add supply, what's going to happen to demand? But those are the basic pieces. I think you can start pretty linear like acquiring customers, they're activating, retaining and generating contribution margin typically would be the output. But where it gets really interesting is we start making it non-linear. So the most basic example of this would be virality. Your existing customers are referring new customers and those go on to refer new customers. Based on that coefficient, it has a lot to do with how fast your business grows.
turns.zh: 而然后一个点击之外会是为市场生意建这个。所以现在我们聊的大多是建模像生意的需求侧。所以现在你也想供给获取和留存、以及这两侧怎么互动。所以当我们加供给，需求会发生啥？但那些是基本块。我觉得你能开始相当线性像获取客户、他们激活、留存、生成贡献毛利通常会是输出。但它在哪变真有趣是我们开始让它非线性。所以最基本例子会是病毒式。你现存客户在推荐新客户、而那些继续推荐新客户。基于那个系数，它很多关于你生意增长多快。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And similarly with paid marketing, as you generate contribution margin, you can reinvest that and grow and actually if you link those two up explicitly, it makes it really clear why thinking about something like payback period is a much better measure of paid marketing performance than LTV to CAC because the speed at which you get enough money back to then go acquire another customer has much more bearing on how fast your business can grow than just the raw kind of [inaudible 00:09:39]. This is where it gets really interesting where you get some variables to play with.
turns.zh: 而类似地用付费营销，当你生成贡献毛利，你能再投资它、增长、而其实如果你显式连那两个，它让为啥想回本周期（payback period）是比 LTV 对 CAC 好得多的付费营销表现度量变得极清楚，因为你拿够钱回然后去获取另一个客户的速度，比你生意能增长多快有更多 bearing，而非只是原始那种[听不清 00:09:39]。这是它在哪变真有趣、你有些变量能玩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So let's unpack a bit of the stuff you just talked about. There's a whole decade of knowledge that you just I think collapsed into a couple of minutes. So just to spend a little more time there. So the core three kind of variables to a SaaS business, if you're thinking about the growth model of a SaaS business, for example, you said acquisition channels, where's traffic coming from, and that's essentially how much traffic are you getting, how is it converting and things like that.
turns.zh: 好。所以我们拆一点你刚聊的。有一整个十年的知识你刚我觉得塌缩进几分钟。所以就多花点时间那。所以核心三个变量给 SaaS 生意，如果你在想 SaaS 生意的增长模型，例如，你说获取渠道、流量从哪来、而那本质是你拿多少流量、它怎么转化和类似。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 完全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then there's retention and then there's monetization and multiplying all that together you end up with here's how much revenue you're making as a business. Is that roughly how to think about it?
turns.zh: 然后还有留存，还有变现，把这些都乘在一起，就得出了你这门生意到底赚了多少收入。差不多是这么理解的吧？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, it's roughly right. And those three building blocks are true for here in most businesses. Most of what we're talking about is then nuance on top of that that makes the business unique.
turns.zh: 对，基本没错。而且这三个积木块对绝大多数生意都成立。我们后面聊的大部分内容，都是在它之上做的、让这门生意与众不同的细化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So if someone was just starting the spreadsheet for their SaaS business, and we'll talk about even more examples, but if someone was like, "Here, I'm going to try to figure out my growth model," it's create a row for acquisition channels and traffic you're getting, then a row for roughly your retention rate and then how much you're making per customer. Very high level, is that to think about this?
turns.zh: 好。那假设有人刚开始给自己的 SaaS 生意建一张表格——我们后面还会聊更多例子——但假设有人想『我来试着理清楚我的增长模型』，那就是开一行写获客渠道和流量，再开一行写大概的留存率，然后写每个客户能赚多少。非常宏观地看，是这样想的吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, sweet. And then marketplaces, I think you said that it's transaction over time and average order value. So it's like how many people are buying stuff, how much are they paying each time? And then unit economics per transaction, how much they're making profit per [inaudible 00:10:58].
turns.zh: 好嘞。那市场类生意，我记得你说的是随时间累计的交易量，乘以客单价。就是有多少人在买东西、每次付多少钱？再加上每笔交易的单元经济，也就是每笔能赚多少利润……（听不清）。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And the critical distinction there is for a SaaS business, your marginal costs are often very low. And so it's not an important part to model. But for transactional business, you typically have very high cost or something else that you need to model so [inaudible 00:11:09].
turns.zh: 对，没错。这里关键的区别在于：对 SaaS 生意来说，你的边际成本通常很低，所以建模时它不是重要的一块。但对交易型生意，你通常有很大成本、或者还有别的什么东西需要建模……（听不清）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, because you're just taking a cut and you're not selling software. And then the acquisition channels, retention, monetization, marketplace have those three things just broadly and then plus these additional two elements.
turns.zh: 对，因为你只是抽成，不是在卖软件。然后获客渠道、留存、变现这三件事市场类生意也都有，只不过更宽泛，再加上那两个额外的元素。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah. I think one warning I would give ... so I built these for many businesses. I built them for Thumbtack, at Faire. Many of the companies I worked with, at my consulting firm, they break down in a few places. As soon as you start stacking assumptions, you're highly sensitive to how many assumptions do you have to make and do you know how to make that assumption. And marketplaces kind of create complexity on both of those because for the first piece you're modeling both sides of the business. There's a lot of assumptions. And second, there's a few pieces which are very hard to understand how they work. So the interaction between supply and demand is a big one. Take Amazon as an example. There's a category manager at Amazon who's running their pets business and he decides that he wants to go add a bunch more pet supply to the business. So he's going to go find pet food brands, pet toy brands. Those businesses will generate a bunch of revenue on the Amazon marketplace.
turns.zh: 对。我想给一个提醒……我给很多公司建过这种模型，在 Thumbtack 建过，在 Faire 也建过。我在咨询公司合作过的很多公司，它们会在几个地方出问题。一旦你开始往上叠假设，你就会对『得做多少个假设、你知不知道怎么做这个假设』高度敏感。而市场类生意恰恰在两方面都制造复杂性——第一块你是在给生意的两端建模，假设特别多；第二，有几块东西你其实很难搞懂它们是怎么运作的。供需之间的互动就是个大头。拿亚马逊举例，有个品类经理在管他们的宠物业务，他决定要往里加一大批宠物用品。那他就会去找宠物食品品牌、宠物玩具品牌。这些品牌会在亚马逊市场上产生一大笔收入。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But how much of that was actually incremental? Maybe there's a bunch of existing pet supply that customers would've bought anyway. And does having a bunch more supply create a happier customer who retains longer and drives those cohorts up? These things are very hard to decide, something we've spent a lot of time thinking about in various marketplace businesses. And so if you're not careful, you can have a junk in, junk out problem with marketplaces. So the thing that I have gravitated to more as I've done more of this is one very basic high level conceptual model, so that's like the building blocks you talked about, which as simply as possible describes how the whole system works. And so you start to get a feel for which levers are important.
turns.zh: 但这些里有多少是真正增量？可能本来就有很多现成的宠物用品，客户本来也会买。多了一堆供给，会不会让客户更满意、留存更久、把那些群组拉高？这些事非常难判断，是我们在各种市场类生意里花了很多时间琢磨的东西。所以你一不小心，就会在市场类生意上遇到『垃圾进、垃圾出』的问题。所以我做得越多，越倾向于只用一个非常基础、高层的概念模型——就是咱聊的那个积木块，用尽可能简单的方式把整个系统怎么运转讲清楚。这样你慢慢就能感觉出哪些杠杆是关键的。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And then for each area of the business, so each product pod, each go to market team, they should have their own kind of mini model which describes the piece of the business they're working on. So that team typically has a north star and they should know what are all the inputs that drive that and a little model to articulate how that works. And you'll never kind of stitch this up into one master thing. I think that's a very difficult task. But you have the dual benefit of understanding how the business works broadly and then understanding if you zoom in on this piece, what are the levers i need to be pulling to move my metric.
turns.zh: 然后对每个业务领域，每个产品小队、每个走向市场的团队，都应该有自己的迷你模型，来描述他们负责的那块业务。那个团队通常有个北极星指标，他们应该知道驱动它的所有输入是什么，并有一个小模型来表达它怎么运作。但你永远没法把这些都拼成一份总表——我觉得那是个极难的任务。但你的好处是双重的：既能从宏观上理解生意怎么运转，又能钻进去看这块具体该扳哪些杠杆来推动我的指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make that last point a little more concrete, what's an example of that? What's a team that would have their little model? I imagine every team has their own understanding of how the lever works, but what's an example?
turns.zh: 为了让最后这点更具体，能不能给个例子？什么样的团队会拥有自己的小模型？我想每个团队对自己那块杠杆怎么运作都有自己的理解，但能举个例子吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I think there's probably two core archetypes for this. So if you have something that's more like a growth team, it's a little bit simpler. They're typically managing some kind of funnel and they can understand do I want to work on driving more traffic, more conversion, more retention. Typically, that's a somewhat linear relationship.
turns.zh: 我觉得大概有两种核心原型。如果你是更像增长团队的那种，会简单一点。他们通常在管某种漏斗，能理解自己是该做更多流量、更高转化还是更好留存。通常这是个比较线性的关系。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But then you have all these teams that are really managing some tension in the business, which is totally different than a funnel. So say if you have a marketplace quality team, what they care about is driving some standard for quality for the suppliers on a marketplace, but there's not a linear kind of relationship between working on that kind of problem. So if I let on a bunch of new supply to a marketplace, probably the first thing that happens is our GMV or our revenue goes up because we have all these new suppliers which can transact demand, but if those are on average lower quality, it's going to degrade the kind of customer experience and reduce retention over time. And so the model that they're trying to build is how to manage that tension.
turns.zh: 但还有一类团队，真正在管理生意里的某种张力，这跟漏斗完全不同。比如你有个市场质量团队，他们关心的是给市场上的供给方设定某种质量标准，但在这类问题上发力，跟结果之间不是线性关系。如果我往市场里放一大批新供给，第一件事多半是 GMV 或收入涨了，因为多了这么多能满足需求的供给方；但如果这些供给平均质量更低，长期就会拉低客户体验、减少留存。所以他们想建的模型，是怎么管理这种张力。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Similarly in a FinTech business or many marketplaces now have FinTech elements, you're often underwriting the transaction. That team is thinking about the tension between extending more credit and driving higher spend versus defaults on the other side, like what's the contribution margin maximizing point at which we could offer credit. And so their models are going to look pretty different than what a growth team is managing.
turns.zh: 类似的，在金融科技生意里，或者现在很多市场都带金融科技元素，你常常是在给交易做授信。那个团队在想的，是『扩大信用、推动更高消费』和另一头的『坏账』之间的张力——我们在哪个点对客户提供信用，能让边际贡献最大化？所以他们的模型看起来会跟增长团队管的那些很不一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So you mentioned this idea of archetypes and I was going to ask you when you think about developing a growth model for a company and with Basis One, the company that you ran before Faire, you basically developed these things for startups and how many companies would you say you helped through this process and helped develop growth models for just to [inaudible 00:14:47]?
turns.zh: 明白了。你提到了原型这个点，我本来想问：你在为公司搭建增长模型时——你之前在 Faire 之前创立的 Basis One，基本上就是帮创业公司做这个——你大概帮多少家公司走完了这个流程、建了增长模型，就当是……（听不清）？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: We probably built 20 or 30 these in my time at Basis One.
turns.zh: 我在 Basis One 期间大概建了二三十个这种模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. It's probably more than anyone out there. So I think that's a context to set. You've had more experience doing this than maybe anyone else out there, but we won't compare.
turns.zh: 厉害。这数量可能比外面任何人都多。所以这是要交代的背景：你在这件事上的经验可能比谁都丰富，不过我们不比较了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there archetypes/templates/tools that you have found useful to think about, I'm coming in fresh to think about the growth model for a company. What have you found helpful to get started to lay the groundwork?
turns.zh: 有没有什么原型、模板、工具，是你觉得对『我是新人，要来想一家公司的增长模型』很有用的？你发现什么对起步、打基础有帮助？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: One thing I'll say is going back to 50% of the value being figuring it out, that actually negates the value of templates in some way. You kind of want to build it up for yourself from first principles to understand how the business works. So the more painful the process of building it is, probably the more you're learning. But I do think there's been a lot written on this that you can find online and I think the building blocks I talked about are a useful starting place for how to put these together. I also think Reforge, which is a product in growth school, which we both know has done I think probably the most work to build this into a discipline. And so if you want to go really deep on this, my top recommendation would be to start with Reforge.
turns.zh: 有一点我要说：回到『一半价值在于自己把它想明白』，这话其实在某种程度上否定了模板的价值。你其实更想从第一性原理自己搭出来，去理解生意怎么运作。所以搭的过程越痛苦，你学到的可能越多。但我确实觉得网上已经有很多写这个的文章，而且我说的那些积木块是个好起点。我还觉得 Reforge——咱俩都认识的那家做增长学校的产品——可能是把这件事做成一门学科做得最深入的。所以你想钻得很深的话，我最推荐从 Reforge 入手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So getting even more concrete, you've built a lot of these growth models. What's an actual example of growth model you've built and more specifically what have you learned from the experience of building that growth model at either, I guess, I was going to say a fictional company but let's go with a real company?
turns.zh: 好。再更具体一点：你建过很多这种增长模型。能不能讲一个你实际建过的增长模型例子？更具体地说，你从建那个模型（在真实公司，不说虚构的了）的经历里学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: One of the immediate things that you see when you build these is that your growth is much more sensitive to customer retention than you can ever intuit because there's a lot of interaction between having a healthy retained customer base and everything else you care about, which is the rate at which they're referring new customers, generating content, generating contribution margin. And so it quickly makes it clear that actually getting a smaller percentage gain on retention is often much more valuable than making a bigger change in some other area. And as a result you may be misallocating your product and growth resources in a pretty significant way.
turns.zh: 建这种模型时立刻能看到的一件事是：你的增长对客户留存比你能直觉到的敏感得多，因为健康的留存客户群和你关心的其他一切之间互动很强——比如他们推荐新客户的速度、产出内容、产生边际贡献的速度。所以它很快就能讲清楚：在留存上拿到一个百分比更小的小增益，往往比在别的领域做大改动有价值得多。结果就是，你可能正以相当严重的方式错配了你的产品和增长资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your point there is really important that the more you work on this stuff, the more you will learn what actually is movable and the expected ROI on investments. For founders that are just getting started on this sort of stuff, do you have any just general advice or guidance on okay, retention is probably going to be very hard to move, don't expect that metric even though it's your point that it's often the biggest lever? Any just general guidance of here's where you probably will see impact, maybe you should now count on a ton. How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 你这点说得太关键了：你在这上做得越多，越能学到什么真的能推动、以及投资的预期回报。对刚起步的创始人，有没有什么总体建议？比如『留存很可能非常难推动，别指望那个指标』——尽管你说的它是最大杠杆。有没有个总体指引，说『大概能在哪看到效果、哪别指望太多』？你是怎么想的？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I think one tactical piece of advice, I think the best way to start this is to find a smart analyst or smart finance person often is the right type of person to partner with and just start building it. So you may have some intuition around this for the core operating model the business is running. This is a little bit different. You need to start building in more variables but I would start there and start iterating on the model. And I think this process of where you have leverage to move it is very hard to intuit. So I think you just have to start and there's a feedback loop between what kind of gains the team is putting up and how that impacts your model and over the course of multiple quarters of iterating on this, you build much more intuition for what works.
turns.zh: 一个实操建议：最好的起步方式是找个聪明的分析师、或者聪明的财务的人——通常是合适的一类搭档——然后就开始建。你对公司核心运营模型可能有些直觉，但这有点不一样，你需要开始纳入更多变量，但我建议就从这起步、去迭代模型。而且『我在哪有杠杆能推动它』这个过程很难靠直觉。所以我觉你就得开始干，团队做出的增益和它怎么影响你的模型之间有个反馈环，经过好几个季度的迭代，你会对什么管用建立起强得多的直觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So say that somebody has been listening to this episode, maybe they've heard it, they've listened to it three times now and they're just like, "Hey, I got a model that kind of feels like the beginnings of something." What do you do once you have a growth model? How does it actually inform what you do as a startup?
turns.zh: 好。假设有人一直在听这期，可能已经听三遍了，然后想『嘿，我有个模型，感觉像是点眉目了』。有了增长模型之后该干嘛？它到底怎么指导你作为创业公司去做事？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: It's very helpful input into a quarterly or annual planning process. It depends a little bit on the stage of the company, but say you're at the stage where you have maybe 10 or 20 product pods which are allocated across various parts of the business and you're going through annual planning. Often you want to do a zero based accounting exercise where we say we want to from the ground up decide how those people should spend their time and there's some kind of pod allocation exercise where we're deciding which places those go to. The most difficult thing about making that kind of effort is developing a common currency by which you can trade off their efforts. So this team is saying they can move this metric by X and this team is moving this metric by Y. I have no way to make those two things comparable. The growth model is the function that lets you do that.
turns.zh: 它对季度或年度规划是非常有用的输入。这有点看公司阶段，但假设你到了有 10 到 20 个产品小队、分布在业务各处的阶段，正在做年度规划。你常常想做一次零基核算，从底层重新决定这些人时间该怎么花，还有某种小队分配的动作，决定资源去哪。这种努力最难的地方，是建立起一种通用货币，让你可以权衡不同团队的努力。这个团队说能把这个指标推 X，那个团队说能推 Y。我没办法把这两件事放一起比。增长模型就是让你能做这件事的那个函数。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And so you can have this analyst or this finance person we talked about who is operating this model work with the product managers to run those scenarios through this model and generate it into a common currency. So now we have a spreadsheet that says these are the things we could work on. This is roughly how it will impact our short or long-term growth. Now you have the ability to make much better kind of allocation decisions. So that would be at the most macro level. And I think the more micro one is for an individual product pod, I have this north star goal, which levers should I be pulling? They should be using their mini models to make that assessment. If you look at the strategy doc for a product group or team, I think that having a model like this should be a core part of that because that way they can articulate what it is they actually [inaudible 00:19:18].
turns.zh: 所以你可以让咱说的那个分析师或财务，去运作这个模型、跟产品经理合作，把那些情景跑进模型里，换算成通用货币。于是我们有张表写着：这些是我们可以考虑做的事，这大致会怎么影响我们的短期或长期增长。现在你就能做更好的资源分配决策了。这是最宏观的层面。更微观的层面是：对一个产品小队，我有这个北极星目标，我该扳哪些杠杆？他们应该用各自的小模型来做这个判断。你看一个产品组或团队的战略文档，我觉得这种模型应该是核心部分，因为他们就能说清自己到底……（听不清）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you found a model doing this exercise, coming up with a growth model for a company or a startup you've worked with, radically shifted the way they think? Is there an example that comes to mind of, "Oh wow, we came up with this," and they're like they didn't even know this was a huge lever and that changed the way they approached growth.
turns.zh: 你有没有遇到过，做了这个建模、给某个公司或创业公司想出增长模型后，彻底改变了他们的思维方式？有没有这种『哇，我们想出了这个』、他们之前压根不知道这是个巨大杠杆、从而改变了增长打法的例子？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I mean the first time this was very eye-opening to me and probably the first one I built was the one we built at Thumbtack in partnership with our finance team, and it made it so immediately obvious that we were exceptionally sensitive to the repeat rate of new customers. If you think about Thumbtack, we offered a thousand categories. This is a local services marketplace for people to hire electricians or plumbers or wedding planners. Almost all the traffic came from a very targeted SEM or SEO on a specific thing. So they hired [inaudible 00:20:01].
turns.zh: 嗯，我第一次做这个事对我就特别开眼界，大概也是我建的第一个，是我们在 Thumbtack 跟财务团队合作建的那个。它立刻就把一件事摆得明明白白：我们对新客户的复购率异常敏感。你想 Thumbtack，我们提供上千个品类，是个本地服务市场，让人雇电工、水管工或婚礼策划。流量几乎都来自对某个具体品类的精准 SEM 或 SEO。所以他们雇了……（听不清）。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Initially, it was very hard for us to then go upsell you into something else, but the rate at which we did that made all the difference because it radically changed the LTV of that customer, which then fed back into how much we could go pay to acquire new customers. And so we had a team that was primarily focused on optimizing that initial flow. So SEO and conversion rate. We shipped hundreds of experiments to increase our conversion rate. We had done much less on the life cycle piece like how do we cross sell you into these other things. Building this model helped us internalize that we needed to shift a bunch of resources from top of funnel to deeper in the stack and that ultimately let us build a much better customer journey.
turns.zh: 一开始，我们很难再向上销售给你别的东西，但我们做这件事的速率起了决定性作用，因为它彻底改变了那个客户的 LTV，而 LTV 又回过头决定我们能花多少钱去获客。所以我们当时有个团队主要专注优化那个初始流程——SEO 和转化率。我们上线了几百个实验来提高转化率。而在生命周期那块——比如怎么交叉销售给你别的东西——我们做得少得多。建这个模型帮我们内化了一件事：我们需要把一批资源从漏斗顶部挪到更深的环节，最终让我们建出了好得多的客户旅程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Your point about retention being one of the biggest levers reminds me at Airbnb there's like a data dive once where a data scientist found that same conclusion. "Man, if we move retention by 1%, we're going to hit all our goals." And we tried and it was just very hard. And I'm curious, how often do you find that you can actually meaningfully move retention or is there anything that you've found to be effective in increasing retention for many of the companies that you've worked at?
turns.zh: 好。你说留存是最大杠杆之一，让我想起 Airbnb 有一次数据深挖，一个数据科学家得出同样结论：『天，只要把留存动 1%，我们所有目标都达标。』我们试了，结果特别难。我好奇：你有多常发现真的能有意义地推动留存？或者你对合作过的很多公司，有没有什么被证明有效的提升留存的办法？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Retention is a tough measure to work on because it is the culmination of the entire product experience. Whether people come back or not has to do with everything that they experienced along the way. And so I think that the primary advice is actually if you were trying to remove a retention style metric, rarely should you go right to the source and send them more email or push notification or something like that. It's really actually about understanding what is the customer experience and what matters to them. And in a marketplace context, it's often depth of supply or the interaction they have with supply. So you actually should be working more on core product levers than you are on, call it, growth product levers to move retention. So it's a deep understanding of that customer journey and where you actually have the opportunity to improve it.
turns.zh: 留存是个难啃的指标，因为它是整个产品体验的集大成。人回不回来，跟他们一路上经历的一切都有关。所以我的首要建议其实是：如果你想改善一个留存类指标，很少应该直接奔着源头去、给他们多发邮件或推送通知之类的。真正要做的，是理解客户的体验是什么、什么对他们重要。在市场语境下，往往就是供给的深度、或者他们跟供给的互动。所以你其实应该更多在核心产品杠杆上发力，而不是在所谓增长产品杠杆上发力去推留存。这是对客户旅程的深度理解，以及你到底在哪有机会去改善它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you can share any idea or any example comes to mind, what's one of the biggest successes you've seen in increasing retention?
turns.zh: 能不能分享一个你印象里、或者想到的点子或例子——你见过在提升留存上最大的成功之一是什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Very often I think the biggest wins in retention come from inflecting the early user experience. So if you're at three, six, twelve months out, usually a customer has formed a pretty strong opinion about whether or not they like this product and they have a pretty good understanding of it. But in that very first experience, you have a lot of opportunity to teach them about why this is a valuable product and kind of prove to them that it's valuable. So the experiments that have been most effective have been typically focused on very early life cycle, and one really valuable lens is to look for variability in that experience. So for the first week or month, which customers are having a bad experience but shouldn't be.
turns.zh: 我觉得留存的很大胜利，常常来自扭转早期用户体验。到第三、第六、第十二个月，客户通常已经对喜不喜欢这产品形成了相当固定的看法，也理解得挺好了。但在那第一次体验里，你有很多机会去教他们为什么这产品有价值、并向他们证明它确实有价值。所以最有效的实验通常聚焦在非常早期的生命周期，一个很有价值的视角是去找这次体验里的波动——在第一周或第一个月，哪些客户体验很差、但其实本不该差。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So if you take Lyft or Uber, for example, an Uber driver signs up for the service. Some of them just by luck of the draw are going to make a pretty bad hourly rate because a customer canceled on them or they were just in a low density area, and there was some problem with their experience. That driver doesn't know that's not how it works. They might think, "I just make $3 an hour on this platform," and they're never going to come back. And so if you can target streamlining that experience or homogenizing that experience, it's typically very helpful. This is why you see both of those companies dueling it out to guarantee the highest first first week or first month earning. What they're trying to do is prove to you that this is what the experience is going to be like longer term, and you pull up all those below average first experiences to average and drive much better retention curves going forward.
turns.zh: 拿 Lyft 或 Uber 举例：一个 Uber 司机注册了。其中有些人纯粹运气不好，时薪会很差——因为乘客取消了、或者他们就在低密度区域、体验出了点问题。那个司机不知道这不是常态。他可能想『我在这平台上一小时就赚 3 块』，然后就再也不回来了。所以如果你能针对地把那个体验理顺、或者拉平，通常特别有帮助。这就是为什么你会看到这两家公司打来打去，都要保证第一周或第一个月最高收入。他们想做的，是向你证明长期体验就是这样，然后把那些低于平均的首次体验都拉到平均线，从而推高后续的留存曲线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Such a great example and story. It makes me think about this work that I imagine every company ends up doing, which is what are leading indicators of future retention. I'm curious if you've had success doing that. I find there's always these obvious things that you can't do much about to increase retention down the road and there's always this idea of building some ML model that's like anticipating retention based on some behaviors that someone takes. Have you had any experience, any success with those sorts of investments?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这例子和故事真好。它让我想到一种我觉得每家公司最后都会做的工作——就是未来留存的先行指标是什么。我好奇你在这方面成没成功过。我发现总有些明显的事你其实没法做太多去提升未来留存，也总有个想法说建个 ML 模型、根据某人某些行为来预测留存。你在这种投入上有没有过经验、成没成功过？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I think one of the most common analytical failure modes is this pattern, which is our best users do X, so why can't we make other users do that same thing and then drive future attention. It almost never works that way because there's something unique about that customer and their experience which is driving it. And so these correlational exercises, I put very little weight in because I've rarely been able to move Bucket B into the better Bucket A, for example. So I think it's much more about understanding where the real drivers of value are, how to create that really good first round experience to prove to them.
turns.zh: 我觉得最常见的分析失败模式之一就是这种套路：我们最好的用户会做 X，那为啥不能让别的用户也做同样的事，从而推动未来的注意力？它几乎从不是这样运作的，因为那个客户和他体验里有什么独特的东西在驱动它。所以这种相关性练习，我给的权重极低，因为我很少能把 B 组搬到更好的 A 组去。所以我觉得更要紧的是理解价值真正的驱动在哪、怎么创造出那个很好的第一轮体验去向他们证明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And it's interesting that onboarding comes up a lot on these conversations, just the power of onboarding and how much effect that has down the road.
turns.zh: 好。有意思的是，这些对话里『新用户引导』总是被反复提到——引导的威力，以及它对后续有多大影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To your point, people often want to increase retention by focusing on people about to turn and this is a great reminder that your biggest lever is early on when they're just experiencing for the first time.
turns.zh: 顺着你说的，人们常想通过盯着快流失的人来提升留存，这个点子提醒得好：你最大的杠杆其实在最早期，当他们第一次体验的时候。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So yeah, the flip side is absolutely true, right? Working on early user experience is highly impactful. You often see product teams say we should work on resurrection because we have this huge pool of users that is churned out. If we get just 1% of those people back, it's going to be such a big lift. The problem is that pool of users is the group of people who has tried the product and decided they don't want to use it and so it's very hard to convince them otherwise. It's usually much higher leverage to focus on new users and, as a result, typically you want to wait to spin up resurrection efforts until you've exhausted some of these earlier funnel efforts.
turns.zh: 对，反过来也绝对成立，对吧？做早期用户体验影响力很大。你常看到产品团队说，我们应该做『复活』，因为我们有这么一大池子已经流失的用户。只要把其中 1% 拉回来，提升就巨大。问题是那池子的人是试过产品、决定不用的，所以很难说服他们回头。把精力放在新用户上通常杠杆高得多，所以通常你要先把漏斗前面那些努力用尽，再启动复活动作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I want to transition a bit to talking about marketplaces. I honestly can't think of anyone that's worked on more marketplace companies than you. Maybe Jeff Jordan at a16z who's invested in Airbnb and worked at eBay and OpenTable and these companies. But I feel you have so much insight into how to grow and run a marketplace and so I'm really excited to dig in to stuff here.
turns.zh: 我想转个话题聊市场。说实话我想不出有谁比你在更多市场公司干过。也许 a16z 的 Jeff Jordan——投了 Airbnb、在 eBay 和 OpenTable 干过——但我觉得你对怎么增长和运营市场有太多洞见，所以我很兴奋能深挖这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My first question, just why are you excited about marketplaces? What gets you continuously interested in working on marketplaces and why are they such interesting and good businesses?
turns.zh: 我第一个问题，就是为什么你对市场这么兴奋？是什么让你持续对市场感兴趣，为什么它们是这么有趣、这么好的生意？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Why is a marketplace a good business? The first thing is it's like a perfect fit for the venture model, which is why everybody's so interested in them, right? They're very hard to get started, super capital intensive to get started, but once they're rolling, they're very hard to stop. You get this kind of compounding defensibility and gains that makes them very hard to stop. And, as a result, as a marketplace grows, you see these crazy things in the metrics which you don't see for most other businesses. So typically, as you acquire more and more customers, you're acquiring the marginally good fit customer over time and your CACs go up, your LTVs go down, it gets harder and harder.
turns.zh: 为什么市场是个好生意？第一，它跟风投模型是绝配，这也是为什么人人都对它这么感兴趣，对吧？起步非常难、起步极烧钱，可一旦跑起来，就很难停下。你会得到这种复利式的防御力和收益，让它们很难停下。结果就是，随着市场增长，你会在指标里看到别的大多数生意看不到的疯狂现象。通常，你获客越多，随着时间推移你获的是边际上越贴合的客户，于是 CAC 上升、LTV 下降，越来越难。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Marketplace is actually the inverse. The supply liquidity is improving, the experience is improving. So often actually as you see later cohorts in marketplaces, CAC goes down, LTV goes up. You see this crazy inversion where the business gets better and better over time. And so that's I think one of the reasons they're such great businesses. I think to your question on why they're fun to work on, I think everything is just harder. Every question is more complex and so that's made them I think really fun to work on for me.
turns.zh: 市场其实是反过来的。供给的流动性在改善，体验在改善。所以你常看到，市场里越后面的群组，CAC 下降、LTV 上升。你会看到这种疯狂的反转：生意随着时间越来越好。所以我觉得这是它们成为好生意的原因之一。至于你问为什么做起来有趣，我觉得是一切都更难。每个问题都更复杂，所以对我来说做起来真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's interesting coming back to your first point about marketplaces are hard to start, but once they're started they become cheaper to grow and you build moats and work effects. It feels like you as a advisor and person that works on marketplaces, the same thing happens. The fact that you've worked at so many marketplaces makes it more interesting and fun I imagine because you've seen so much of this and so many people haven't experienced this, and so there's almost a Dan Hockenmaier network effect.
turns.zh: 有意思的是回到你第一点——市场难起步，但一旦起步，增长就更便宜，你建起护城河和网络效应。感觉作为做市场咨询和实战的你，同样的事也在发生。你做过这么多市场，让它更有意思、更有趣——我猜是因为你见过这么多，而很多人没经历过，所以简直有个『Dan Hockenmaier 网络效应』。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I appreciate that. I mean I think there's a few folks in this community who've worked with a bunch of marketplace, and you start to see the same topics over and over. So it's really fun to riff with that group on these topics.
turns.zh: 谢谢。我是说这个圈子里有几位做过一堆市场的人，你会反复看到同样的课题。所以跟那群人就这些话题即兴发挥特别好玩。

turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Eppo. Eppo is a next generation A/B testing platform built by Airbnb alums for modern growth teams. Companies like Netlify, Contentful and Cameo rely on Eppo to power their experiments. Wherever you work, running experiments is increasingly essential, but there are no commercial tools that integrate with a modern growth team stack. This leads to waste of time building internal tools or trying to run your experiments through a clunky marketing tool. When I was at Airbnb, one of the things that I loved about our experimentation platform was being able to easily slice results by device, by country, and by user stage.
turns.zh: 本期由 Eppo 赞助。Eppo 是下一代 A/B 测试平台，由 Airbnb 老将打造，面向现代增长团队。Netlify、Contentful、Cameo 这类公司都靠 Eppo 来驱动实验。无论你在哪工作，跑实验都越来越不可或缺，但市面上没有能和现代增长团队技术栈集成的商用工具。这导致要么浪费时间自建内部工具，要么用笨重的营销工具跑实验。我在 Airbnb 时，最喜欢我们实验平台的一点，就是能轻松按设备、国家、用户阶段切分结果。

And Eppo supports tests on the front end, the back end, email marketing and even machine learning clients. Check out Eppo at geteppo.com, geteppo.com and 10X your experiment velocity.
