turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so we're thinking about marketplaces. One of the biggest questions people ask about marketplaces is how do you know if they're going well? What are health metrics? What are KPIs that you find are most helpful to think about when evaluating the health of a marketplace?
turns.zh: 好，我们继续想市场。关于市场，人们问得最多的问题之一就是：你怎么知道它走得好不好？有什么健康指标？评估市场健康度时，你觉得最有用的 KPI 是什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I can give you a couple of pretty obvious ones or basic ones and a couple that are a little bit more nuanced. So that in that first bucket, certainly you need to look at some measure of GMV or transactions. You need something that brings together both the supply and demand side to make sure it's working and that's typically your ultimate north star of which everything else ladders up to.
turns.zh: 我可以给你几个挺明显、基础的，再加几个稍微细腻点的。第一桶里，你当然得看某种 GMV 或交易量的衡量。你需要一个把供需两端都合在一起的东西，确保它在运转，而它通常就是你终极的北极星，其他一切都往上归。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I think the second would be a deep understanding of unit economics because the dynamic I talked about where they're hard to get started means that most marketplace in the early days have pretty poor or maybe even negative unit economics. Instacart famously was losing the money on every order. Uber was losing money on every drive. And so I think understanding that and the components that lead up to it is a very important part of understanding your marketable. So those would be the two kind of obvious ones.
turns.zh: 我觉得第二是对单元经济的深度理解，因为我说的『起步难』那个动态意味着，多数市场在早期单元经济都很差，甚至可能是负的。Instacart  famously 每单都在亏钱。Uber 每趟都在亏钱。所以理解这一点、以及构成它的那些成分，是理解你市场健康度很重要的一部分。这俩就是比较明显的。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I think other two that I would look at beyond that, number one is liquidity. And this is a really broad term that people define in a bunch of different ways. The definition I would give is how reliable is the marketplace? If the consumer is looking for something or supplier is looking to sell something, how often can they do that thing that they're trying to do? And ideally you want to express this metric in the form of a dimension or a type of product experience that a customer really cares about. So for Uber or Lyft, wait time is a classic example. As you add more supply, the average wait time for a customer goes down and there's some magic moment around four or five minutes where it really clicks and is now just a much better service than calling a traditional taxi or something else.
turns.zh: 在这之上我还会看另外两个。第一是流动性。这是个很宽泛的词，大家定义五花八门。我的定义是：市场有多可靠？如果消费者在找某样东西、或供给方想卖某样东西，他们有多大概率能做成想做的事？理想情况下，你要把这个指标表达成客户真正在乎的某种维度、或某种产品体验形态。对 Uber 或 Lyft，等待时间就是经典例子。你加越多供给，客户平均等待时间越短，到大约四到五分钟有个 magic moment，一下子就通了，比叫传统出租车之类好太多。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: For a commerce market, typically it's some form of conversion rate or search to fail metrics. So if I go look for this thing on Amazon, how often can I find it and convert? And so by articulating what the customer cares about and where this threshold is, you can tell when you have a liquid marketplace and essentially until you have a liquid marketplace, really nothing else matters. So this should be the primary thing you're focused on defining and then building towards, and this is why you hear a lot of advice to marketplaces to basically cut scope down to a specific geography or a specific category so you can focus on generating liquidity in that area before you can then scale it elsewhere. So this is the number one, I think, metric for a marketplace.
turns.zh: 对电商市场，通常是某种转化率、或『搜了没找到』的指标。所以我去亚马逊找这个东西，多大概率能找到并下单？通过说清客户在乎什么、以及那个阈值在哪，你就能判断自己是不是有流动性的市场；而本质上，在你有流动性市场之前，别的什么都不重要。所以这应该是你首要聚焦去定义、然后去建设的东西。这也是为什么你会听到很多建议说市场要先把范围砍到某个地理区域或某个品类，好让你在那个区域先做出流动性，再往外扩。所以我觉得这是市场头号指标。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And then the last one I'll give is share of wallet. So this is effectively for your buyer, how much of their total spend are you getting on your marketplaces versus the alternatives. For your seller, how much of the business that they're doing is you versus others? So for Uber drivers, if they spend X amount of hours driving per week, how much are you getting versus Lyft or Door Dash or something else? For a retailer on Faire, if they're buying to stock their store, how much of the product on their shelf came from Faire versus from somewhere else? These are very important metrics for us to understand.
turns.zh: 最后一个我给的是钱包份额。说白了，对买家，你在你市场上拿到他总花费的多少，相对其他替代方案？对卖家，他做的生意里有多少是你、而不是别人？对 Uber 司机，如果他一周开 X 小时，你拿到多少、相对 Lyft 或 DoorDash 之类？对 Faire 上的零售商，他进货补店时，货架上多少来自 Faire、多少来自别处？这些对我们都非常重要。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: One, for the obvious reason that as it goes up, your LTVs go up and you have a much better business. But probably more importantly than that, the higher it is, the less likely a customer is to multi-tenant, meaning use another marketplace or another service. And ideally you want that customer to commit to using just this marketplace and the higher share of wallet is the more likely that is. But I will say that it's very hard typically to get this to happen on both sides of the marketplace simultaneously. So often you have to pick your leverage point, which one do you think you can actually drive very high share of wallet on.
turns.zh: 一，原因很直白：它越高，你的 LTV 越高、生意越好。但可能比这更重要的是，它越高，客户越不可能多平台并用，也就是用别的市场或服务。理想情况下你想让客户承诺只用这一个市场，钱包份额越高，这件事越可能发生。但我要说，通常很难让市场两端同时发生这种事。所以你常得挑你的杠杆点——你觉得哪一端真能把钱包份额推得很高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So just to summarize, the metrics that you find to be most helpful in tracking marketplace health, there's these two that are just general business health metrics, GMV and unit economics. Then I think what's most unique to marketplaces, which is liquidity and essentially it's just like how often are people having a good time on both sides of the marketplace? And I love the way you broke it up like for Uber it would be how quickly do you get a car. For most marketplaces, it's just like what percentage of the time do you get something that you want, fill rate basically. And then share a wallet, which to me feels like ... even again going back to the first kind of bucket of just broadly this business going well, do you think about that separately versus just business growth and how much we're making, do you feel like share of wallet is a different category of metric?
turns.zh: 好。总结一下，你觉得追踪市场健康度最有用的指标：有两个是通用生意健康指标，GMV 和单元经济。然后我觉得最市场专属的，是流动性——本质就是供需两端有多大比例在『玩得开心』？我喜欢你这种拆法：对 Uber 就是多快能叫到车；对多数市场，就是有多大比例时间能拿到想要的东西，基本就是满足率。然后是钱包份额，对我来说感觉像……又回到第一桶那种广义的『生意走得好』，你是把它单另想、还是就跟生意增长、我们赚多少放一起？你觉得钱包份额是个不同类别的指标吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I do think share of wallet is different for this reason. If you could tell me we could grow GMV 10% by getting 10% more customers or by getting 10% more of our current customers' wallet, I would take the latter because you now have a deeper relationship with them, which tells you something more about the future retention and defensibility of the marketplace. So I think it's basically a measure of depth rather than breadth. And I will take depth every time in a marketplace.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得钱包份额不同，原因是：如果你告诉我，我们可以通过多 10% 客户把 GMV 涨 10%，或者通过多拿现有客户 10% 的钱包把 GMV 涨 10%，我选后者。因为你现在跟他们关系更深，这能告诉你关于未来留存和市场防御力的更多信息。所以我觉得它基本是深度的衡量，而不是广度。而在市场里，我每次都选深度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You worked on consumer and B2B marketplaces and so I'm curious, do you find share of wallet is important on both types of marketplaces or is it a lot more important in B2B?
turns.zh: 好。你做过消费类和 B2B 市场，所以我好奇，你觉得钱包份额在这两类市场都重要，还是 B2B 重要得多？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So you typically have some form of business on the supply side of a marketplace. Maybe it's a pseudo business that's effectively a consumer, but you can almost always measure some form of share of wallet on the supply side of a marketplace no matter what. On the consumer side, if you're a B2B marketplace, you typically have a cleaner share of wallet metric, but it's not always the case for consumer businesses.
turns.zh: 你通常在市场供给端都有某种生意。也许是个本质是消费者的伪生意，但几乎不管怎样，你总能量到供给端某种形式的钱包份额。在消费端，如果你是个 B2B 市场，你通常有个更干净的钱包份额指标，但消费类生意不总是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. And again, just to clarify share of wallet, it's essentially percentage of spend in, say, a problem space that they're giving to you. So for Faire, it'd be like the retailers, what percentage of their vendors come through Faire?
turns.zh: 好。再澄清下钱包份额，它本质就是——在某个问题领域里，他们花的钱有多少给了你。对 Faire，就是零售商，他们多大比例的供应商走 Faire？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Exactly. If you look at their shelf in their store, what percentage of that shelf came from Faire versus something else?
turns.zh: 对。你看他们店里的货架，有多大比例是来自 Faire、而不是别处？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Another constant question marketplace founders have is whether they should focus on supply or demand. And I know it's never black and white, but do you have any general advice on where to focus?
turns.zh: 好。市场创始人另一个永恒的问题是：该聚焦供给还是需求？我知道这从来不是非黑即白，但你有没有总体建议说该聚焦哪？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah. I mean the answer is obviously both to some extent. I think you can't ignore either side. I do think though that on average when you hear advice about where to focus, people over rotate on supply and actually are under focused on demand. And I think there's a couple of reasons for this. One is supply is disproportionately important early on because it is the product. Until you have enough supply, you don't have anything and so you do have to focus on it to a high degree early on. And two is often the supply side of marketplace is using the product more deeply. There's more product surface area and you need more product resources on the supply side.
turns.zh: 有。答案显然在某种程度上是两者都要，我觉得哪边都不能忽略。但我的确觉得，平均来看，当你听到该聚焦哪边的建议，人们过度偏供给、其实对需求关注不够。我觉得原因有几个。一是供给在早期不成比例地重要，因为它就是产品。在你供给足够之前，你啥都没有，所以早期你确实得高度聚焦供给。二是市场的供给端往往用产品用得更深，产品表面积更大，你在供给端需要更多产品资源。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: However, I think this tricks people into thinking that that's the optimization function or you think you should think more about supply. I think ultimately demand is the only thing that matters. If you are successful at aggregating the demand in your industry, you will have the winning marketplace. Because if you go to a supplier, a restaurant or an electrician or a driver and say, "I have this customer for you that I can give to you at a rate that's going to make you money," they're always going to say yes. And so demand is the currency. And so when you think about trade-offs or how to optimize a business, I think taking the perspective of the customer or the demand side is always the right one.
turns.zh: 但这会骗人以为那就是优化函数、以为你该多想供给。我觉得最终需求才是唯一要紧的。如果你成功聚合了你行业里的需求，你就有了赢的市场。因为如果你去找一个供给方——餐馆、电工、司机——说『我这有个客户，我能以让你赚钱的费率给你』，他们永远会说好。所以需求是货币。所以当你想权衡、或怎么优化一门生意，我觉得站在客户、也就是需求侧的视角永远是对的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's a really important nuance here, and there's actually a little mini Twitter debate with Bill Gurley I think a while ago where he made the same point that in the end, the most important thing you got to get right is aggregate all the demand. You need to become the place people come to transact in that space. But oftentimes the way you do that is acquire supply that is hard to acquire. And so would you agree with that? Often it's just, yes, prioritize the customer experience, but that may be you need to spend most of your time acquiring supply so that they're happy.
turns.zh: 我觉得这里有个很重要的细微差别，其实之前跟 Bill Gurley 在推特上有过一场小辩论，他点了同样的点：最终你最该做对的，是聚合所有需求。你得成为人们来那个领域交易的地方。但常常你做到这点的方法，是去获取那些难获取的供给。所以你同意这点吗？往往就是：对，优先客户体验，但那可能意味着你得把大部分时间花在获取供给上，好让他们开心。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Absolutely. And the culmination of those two points is you only should acquire supply to the extent you understand how it impacts demand. So, for example, if we go back to this liquidity metric, there is some point for a market for Uber where you don't want more supply because you're no longer reducing wait times or doing something that improves the customer experience in a meaningful way. And similarly to the kind of pet store example on Amazon, there's some amount of supply where you're probably no longer incrementally improving the pet buyer's experience and so it's probably not worth investing those dollars. So supply is critically important, but it has to be framed from what is the customer benefit that I'm driving.
turns.zh: 绝对同意。这两点的汇合是：你只应该在『理解它怎么影响需求』的范围内去获取供给。所以回到流动性指标，对 Uber 这种市场，存在某个点，你不再想要更多供给，因为你不再降低等待时间、或不再做任何有意义改善客户体验的事。类似亚马逊宠物店的例子，存在某个供给量，你可能不再增量改善宠物买家的体验，那可能就不值得花那笔钱。所以供给极其重要，但它必须框定为：我在驱动什么客户收益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And another way to put that is what's the biggest constraint to your marketplace's growth, right?
turns.zh: 换个说法就是：你市场增长的头号约束是什么，对吧？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: While we're on that topic, do you have any just rough heuristic that you use to understand which side is most constrained? This may be a big question that isn't answerable in a short answer, but any thoughts there?
turns.zh: 借着这话题，你有没有什么粗略的启发式方法，用来判断哪边最受约束？这可能是个大问题、没法短答，但有什么想法吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: One is I've actually become less and less focused on pure marketplace balance metrics. They're important to monitor, so ratio of buyers to sellers, some of these other things. But actually the thing that matters is can you write an ROI equation for acquiring supply and demand which fully internalizes the marketplace dynamic. So what I mean by this is if you're acquiring a new customer, you need to include the CAC of acquiring that customer, but also the CAC of acquiring the supply for that customer to purchase, which is based on some ratio between the two.
turns.zh: 一个是，我其实越来越不聚焦纯市场平衡指标。它们要监控，比如买家对卖家的比例、那些别的。但真正要紧的是：你能不能给获取供给和需求各写一个 ROI 方程式，把市场动态完全内化进去。我的意思是：如果你获一个新客户，你要算获这个客户的 CAC，也要算为这个客户去购买而获取供给的 CAC——后者基于两者之间某个比例。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And similarly on the supply side, that business can't make a sale unless you also acquire the customer to transact with them. And so if you have dual-sided ROI equations which are appropriately capturing this dynamic, actually I think you can somewhat ignore marketplace balance and just push your acquisition all the way out to the payback period that you're comfortable with on either side. I think the one exception to this would be are there externalities which you can't capture in this equation. So for example, if you have too little demand for Uber drivers, at some point do they just become disillusioned with the service, switch to Lyft, talk badly about it on social media. You do have to look out for extreme low supply or demand scenarios. But generally my view is build really strong ROI models that account for this and then just push to your threshold.
turns.zh: 反过来在供给端也一样，那门生意除非你也获取了跟它交易的客户，否则卖不出去。所以如果你有双向的 ROI 方程式、恰当地捕捉了这个动态，我觉得你其实可以某种程度上忽略市场平衡，把获客一路推到你两边都能接受的回收期阈值。我觉得唯一的例外是：有没有这个方程式捕捉不了的外部性。比如 Uber 司机这边需求太少，到某个点他们会不会就对服务幻灭、转去 Lyft、在社交媒体上说坏话。你确实得留意极端的低供给或低需求情形。但总的来说我的看法是：建真正强的、能算进这个动态的 ROI 模型，然后就推到你的阈值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like the sound of these ROI models. Do you have any guidance for folks to come up with these models in some way? Or is that a whole master class of its own?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这些 ROI 模型这个说法。你有没有什么指引，让人能想出这些模型？还是说这本身就是一整门大师课？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So there's a lot of nuance by business, but the basic formulation is CAC for the side you're focused on. So let's take Uber again, as an example. CAC to acquire a rider and then an additional amount of CAC loaded on for the supply, the drivers that you're acquiring, times the ratio of drivers to supply you're acquiring at that time. So basically, do I need one driver for every 10 passengers? We then take the CAC of that passenger times 10% of a driver. That gives you CAC and then you compare that to the LTV of the customer, and that allows you to calculate payback period.
turns.zh: 按生意不同有很多细节，但基本式是：你聚焦那一侧的 CAC。再用 Uber 举例。获一个乘客的 CAC，加上叠加在供给上的额外 CAC——也就是你获取司机，乘以当时司机对乘客的比例。比如，我是不是每 10 个乘客就需要 1 个司机？那就拿那个乘客的 CAC 乘以 0.1 个司机。这就得到 CAC，然后跟客户 LTV 比，就能算回收期。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Now there's a lot of nuance when you get into an actual marketplace because often they're referring other sides of the marketplace or other things are happening. But that's the basic formulation.
turns.zh: 等你进到真实市场里，会有很多细节，因为它们常常在推荐市场另一端、或有别的事发生。但基本式就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. We should do an actual master class on this formula concoction.
turns.zh: 哇。好。我们应该就这个公式的搭建开一门真正的大师课。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A question I wanted to cover also is I find that for early stage marketplaces, founders sometimes over focus on the theory of marketplaces and how all this stuff that people have put out, including yourself and others, about just how to think about marketplace, all the complexity there. But I find that oftentimes it's simpler just to think of a marketplace like 90 something percent of your success is going to be the same things that any business will have to deal with, growth and profit and retention, all these things. And then there's these additional layers that make a marketplace more complicated. And so just to double click on that last piece, what have you found to be most different about working on a marketplace business versus non-marketplace business?
turns.zh: 我还想聊一个问题：我发现对早期市场，创始人有时过度聚焦市场的理论和人们（包括你和其他人）抛出的那些『怎么思考市场、里面的所有复杂性』。但我觉得常常更简单——想一个市场，你 90% 多的成功会跟任何生意都得面对的东西一样：增长、利润、留存，所有这些。然后才是让市场更复杂的那些额外层。就顺着最后这点展开说：你觉得做市场生意、跟非市场生意，最大的不同在哪？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good question. So I think that effectively every decision you make in a marketplace has a second order consequence that you need to think through and maybe third and fourth order consequences at that. Take something like pricing. It's like this is a pretty complicated topic no matter what, but if you're looking at a SaaS business and you're trying to figure out how to price your subscription, theoretically you can draw a curve which says, "As my price goes up, fewer are going to convert," and so just find the optimal point on that curve where we're managing the tangent between more customers versus more revenue per customer.
turns.zh: 好问题。我觉得在市场里你做的几乎每个决定，都有个你需要想清楚的二阶后果，可能还有三阶、四阶后果。拿定价说。不管怎样这都是个挺复杂的话题，但如果你看一个 SaaS 生意、想搞清楚订阅怎么定价，理论上你能画条曲线说『价格越高，转化越少』，于是就在这条曲线上找最优那点——在『更多客户』和『每客户更多收入』之间管理切线。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But if you take a marketplace, typically you're charging commission on the supply side and their sensitivity to that commission is much harder to understand because, theoretically, if they can transact at a rate that makes them money, they'll sign up all the way to that highest possible commission you could charge. The more you charge, the more you can fund benefits for your customers. So if Amazon charges a higher commission, they can fund more returns and faster shipping for their customers. And so what's the right balance between charging more and maybe kind of discouraging supply from signing up to giving more benefits to demand and encouraging them to sign up?
turns.zh: 但如果是市场，通常你是在供给端抽佣，而他们对佣金的敏感度难懂得多，因为理论上只要他们能以赚钱的费率成交，他们就会一直注册到你能收的最高佣金。你收得越多，就能给客户投越多福利。所以如果亚马逊收更高佣金，就能给客户投更多退货和更快配送。那么『多收钱、可能劝退供给注册』和『给需求更多福利、鼓励他们注册』之间，正确的平衡在哪？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So it's very hard to model that kind of relationship. There's not a simple curve that describes it and so many decisions follow this same pattern. And one lesson I've learned the hard way a bunch of times on this is that if you think about running a marketplace, you're basically a gardener. You have to have a very light touch. If you're building a SaaS business, you're a construction worker, you're building the product and the features and selling it, and it's this very linear thing. For a marketplace, you're messing with this ecosystem that you don't actually really understand how it works. Sometimes you might do something over here which drives this long-term effect two months later and then you're going to be pulling your hair out two months later trying to figure out what you did over here that made that thing happen.
turns.zh: 所以这种关系很难建模，没有一条简单曲线能描述它，很多决定都遵循同样模式。我在这上吃了很多亏学到的教训是：如果你想想运营一个市场，你基本像个园丁。你得有非常轻的触感。如果你在建 SaaS 生意，你是个建筑工，你在建产品和功能、卖它，是非常线性的事。对市场，你是在搅动一个你其实不太懂它怎么运作的生态系统。有时你在这边做点什么，两个月后驱动了个长期效果，然后两个月后你抓狂地想搞清楚当初在这边到底做了什么导致那事发生。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And so I think that the main advice is to tread lightly. When you're messing with the core incentives or mechanisms of a marketplace, be very careful, particularly if you got something that's working on playing with those variables.
turns.zh: 所以我的首要建议是轻着点踩。当你在动市场的核心激励或机制时，要非常小心，尤其是当某个东西正跑得好、你却去玩那些变量时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that metaphor and your point about pricing reminds me ... Your colleague at Faire, Carla Pellicano, she led the pricing recommendations team at Airbnb. It was a team of, I don't know, probably a hundred people that were just dedicated to pricing, figuring out what prices to recommend to hosts, how to get them to adopt these recommendations, building a model to actually come up with the recommendations. And so to your point, pricing is such a complex beast and especially in a marketplace.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个比喻，你说的定价让我想起……你在 Faire 的同事 Carla Pellicano，她在 Airbnb 领导定价推荐团队。那是个我猜上百人的团队，专门做定价——搞清楚该给房东推荐什么价、怎么让他们采纳这些推荐、建个模型真出推荐。所以顺着你说的，定价是这么复杂的怪兽，尤其对市场。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Absolutely. And in general, Carla's been such an incredible force in growing our team and helping us think more rigorously about marketplaces. This is one of the things I mentioned at the start that makes Faire so fun is we've got a lot of people like this that are just so fun to riff with on marketplace problems.
turns.zh: 绝对。总的来说，Carla 在壮大我们团队、帮我们更严谨地思考市场上，是一股了不起的力量。这也是我开头说的、让 Faire 这么好玩的一点：我们有很多这种人，跟他们就市场问题即兴发挥特别开心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many ex-Airbnb people at Faire. It seems to be a magnet for the Airbnb alumni. So whatever you're doing, keep that up.
turns.zh: Faire 有好多 Airbnb 出身的人。它好像是 Airbnb 校友的磁铁。所以不管你在做什么，保持下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another topic that I wanted to chat about is expanding marketplaces and just the idea of thinking about where you expand to with new markets, new verticals, and then also horizontal versus vertical marketplaces. But first, how do you think about the idea of expanding your marketplace once you've got a foothold in a specific area?
turns.zh: 另一个想聊的话题是扩展市场，也就是去想你往哪些新市场、新垂直扩张，还有横向 vs 纵向市场。但先说，一旦你在某个区域站稳了，你是怎么想扩张的？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I've been fortunate to work on marketplaces that are in these massive, massive industries, which is actually true for a lot of marketplaces because they tend to have winner take all dynamics in really big markets. And so you get these really huge [inaudible 00:42:59].
turns.zh: 我很幸运做过的市场都在巨型、巨型行业里，这对很多市场其实成立，因为它们往往在大市场里有赢家通吃的动态。于是你得到这些真正巨大的……（听不清）。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So the local services industry for Thumbtack or the global wholesale industry for Faire, these are meaningful percentages of global GDP. They're huge markets and, as a result, they're really frustrating to work on and also really fun to work on because you have this thing where there's 10 big opportunities that are just one click away from your core business and they all seem really good ideas to do. So how do you actually prioritize between doing those different things? And one thing I've learned here is that actually beyond a certain point, TAM or the size of the market actually matters very little because these are all big enough that they would dramatically inflect the curve of the business if you make them work.
turns.zh: 对 Thumbtack 是本地服务行业，对 Faire 是全球批发行业，这些是全球 GDP 里挺可观的百分比。它们是巨大的市场，结果就是既让人抓狂、又让人兴奋，因为你面临这种局面：核心业务一步之遥就有 10 个大机会，看着都挺好。那你到底怎么在它们之间排优先级？我在这里学到的一点是：过了某个点，TAM 或市场大小其实没那么重要，因为它们都足够大，只要做成了就会剧烈改变生意曲线。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: It's much more relevant to focus on a couple things. One is how adjacent is that to the business as a proxy for can we actually go get it? So if you think about Instacart's setup options, it makes much more sense for them to expand into convenience stores which they have than into traditional retailers because the convenience store looks much more like their current model. The high frequency, shipping speed matters a lot, fulfillment speed matters a lot. And so it's much more likely their current model's going to work there than trying to expand into something else. And that's the right prioritization function for them to think about versus as retail is a slightly bigger market that could be in stores.
turns.zh: 更相关的是聚焦几件事。一是它跟生意有多相邻，作为『我们到底拿不拿得下』的代理。你想 Instacart 的到店自取选项，他们扩到便利店比扩到传统零售商合理得多，因为便利店更像他们现有模型。高频、配送速度很重要、履约速度很重要。所以他们现有模型在那更可能管用，而不是去试别的。对他们来说，这是比『零售是稍大点、可能也做进店』更对的优先级函数。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And the second thing is are there places that you can accentuate your network effect by expanding into new markets. And what I mean by that is are there places where you can use the same supplier or a consumer has demand for multiple things and so it makes your marketplace stronger versus trying to spin up a new network. So for Uber, it makes all the sense in the world to have Uber Eats because, one, they're the same drivers in many cases, but two, the customer wants rides and meals. And so you automatically have this built-in supply base where if they try to do something that was one click further away from this, it would be much less important to them. And so I think that's the way to prioritize new bets.
turns.zh: 第二是：有没有地方你能通过扩到新市场来放大网络效应。我的意思是：有没有地方你能用同一批供给、或者一个消费者有多重需求，从而让你的市场更强，而不是去起一张新网。对 Uber，做 Uber Eats 完全说得通，因为一来很多是同批司机，二来客户既要打车又要吃饭。于是你自动有了内置供给基——如果他们去做离这更远一步的事，那对他们就重要得多。所以我觉得这是排新赌注的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such an interesting point that basically if you're thinking about the upside of a marketplace, think less about just the total TAM of all the adjacent marketplace opportunities in the markets around them and more about how easily it'll be for you to expand into them even if they're smaller.
turns.zh: 这点太有意思了：基本上你想市场上行空间时，少想『周边那些相邻市场机会的总 TAM 加起来多大』，多想『哪怕它们更小，你扩张进去有多容易』。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: There's one other lesson here which I've learned a few times, which is that product is the thing that matters when expanding. So because of this dynamic we talked about where liquidity is so important and there's a race to get there, like the first person, the liquidity wins, you often see this arms race where people will spend a huge amount of money on go to market and incentives to bootstrap the market. And that is an important part of the strategy because it actually does matter who drives liquidity faster.
turns.zh: 这里还有个我学了几回的教训：扩张时，产品才是要紧的东西。因为咱们说的那个动态——流动性太重要、而且有场抢先到位的竞赛，第一名、流动性赢——你常看到这种军备竞赛：人们花巨资在走向市场和激励上、去冷启动市场。而这确实是战略重要的一部分，因为谁更快驱动流动性真的要紧。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But I've learned over and over and over that that's actually not the main thing. It's who can deliver an incredible end-to-end customer experience first, even if for a smaller number of customers. Because that's what creates the flame where actually customers are really loving it, retained, talking about it, and you can then expand from there. So the other big learning from expanding a marketplace is don't let go to market get too far ahead of product. You need to keep those two pieces in lockstep as you're expanding.
turns.zh: 但我一遍又一遍学到，那其实不是主菜。是谁能先交付一个惊艳的端到端客户体验，哪怕客户数更少。因为那才是造出火种的所在——客户真的爱它、留存、口口相传，然后你从那扩出去。所以扩张市场的另一个大教训是：别让走向市场跑得太领先产品。扩张时你得让这两块步调一致。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on a really common piece of advice for marketplaces, which is don't focus on GMV and growth rates and just expansion early on, but instead focus on getting a flywheel going even if it's small, to show that you can make people happy and you can give people what they're looking for. Is there anything you can add there or talk about?
turns.zh: 这触及市场一个很常见的建议：早期别盯 GMV 和增长率、别只顾扩张，而是聚焦先让一个飞轮转起来、哪怕它小，去证明你能让人开心、能给人他们要的东西。你还有什么能补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's exactly right. And the reason this is the right advice is because everything else follows proving you have a good customer experience. Even if you have a very few customers, if your cohorts look really good, they're retaining or even kind of like the classic smiling curve where you see more in engagement later in the life cycle than you do earlier, that's the thing that gives the company conviction to invest resources against it. That's the reason that VCs are going to want to invest rather than a bunch of low quality GMV in a market.
turns.zh: 有，我觉得那完全对。这建议对的原因是：其他一切都跟着『证明你有好客户体验』走。哪怕你客户很少，只要你的群组看着很好——他们在留存，甚至像经典的微笑曲线、生命周期后段参与度比前段还高——那正是给公司信心去投资源的东西。那也是 VC 想投的原因，而不是投一堆低质 GMV。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Speaking of VCs, investing and expanding marketplaces, something that I've noticed is a lot of marketplaces try to find a SaaS business to build on top of their marketplace and find some kind of recurring revenue component and then, in reverse, a lot of SaaS businesses look for how do we add a marketplace to what we're doing. I'm curious how often you find that this actually works out and what do you have to get right to add this other type of business model on top of something that's working.
turns.zh: 好。说到 VC、投资和扩张市场，我注意到的一点是：很多市场想找个 SaaS 生意建在自己上面、找某种经常性收入成分；反过来，很多 SaaS 生意也在找『怎么给我们做的东西加个市场』。我好奇你多久看到这种真成功、以及要在已跑通的东西上叠加另一种商业模式，得做对什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So broadly, I will say I think it's easier for a marketplace to go SaaS than it is the other direction and the reason for that is two things. One is it's a new capability to generate demand, which is fundamentally what a marketplace has to do, and it's a higher value activity. This is why the effective commission of a marketplace, often 10, 15, 20% is much higher than the effective commission of a SaaS business in the 2% to 3% range. So you're just doing much more of the value chain in the marketplace. And second is the marketplace by definition starts with relationships on both sides. But the SaaS business does not have any relationships with the demand side customer. And so they have to acquire a whole new type of demand to make this work.
turns.zh: 总的来说，我会说市场去做 SaaS 比反过来容易，原因有俩。一是它生成需求是个新能力——而那根本就是市场必须做的——而且它是更高价值的活。这也是为什么市场的有效抽佣——常 10、15、20%——远高于 SaaS 生意 2% 到 3% 的范围。所以你在市场里做的是价值链里多得多的部分。二是市场定义上就两端都有关系，而 SaaS 生意跟需求端客户没有任何关系。所以他们得获取一整类全新需求才能成。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: It's not to say it can't work. There's actually a classic kind of SaaS bootstrap to marketplace playbook. This is what OpenTable did. I think we've actually seen some new examples of companies doing this. One in the healthcare space is Solve. They built some interesting products for healthcare clinics that they're now bootstrapping into marketplace. And so I think it's possible, but I think it's very difficult. And then for a marketplace, the lens you should take is much less about how to drive more monetization, but just how do we create a much better experience for our customers because there's some painful thing that they're doing today that we can build for them instead. And so how do we better integrate with the way that they're running their back office or accounting systems is a classic example of where you can make it much better.
turns.zh: 不是说它不可能成。其实有个经典的『SaaS 冷启动到市场』剧本。OpenTable 就是这么干的。我觉得也看到些公司这么做的新例子。医疗领域有个 Solve，他们给诊所建了些有意思的产品，现在正冷启动成市场。所以我觉得可能，但非常难。然后对市场来说，你的视角应该远少想『怎么驱动更多变现』，而只想『我们怎么给客户造好得多的体验』——因为有些他们今天在做的痛苦事，我们可以替他们建出来。所以怎么更好接入他们跑后台或财务系统的方式，就是你能做得好得多的经典例子。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: In the process, you're often making their lives easier, but you're also making your product much stickier. Your retention will go up as a result of this. And so I think if you take the lens of what's the customer pain we're solving, you'll be much more effective than how do we get a few more points of margin out of this customer.
turns.zh: 这过程里，你常让他们生活更轻松，但也让你的产品黏得多。结果你的留存会涨。所以我觉得，如果你取『我们在解决什么客户痛点』这个视角，会比『怎么从这客户多抠几个点的毛利』有效得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If a founder was coming to you and they're like, "Hey Dan, we are a marketplace and we're thinking about adding a SaaS product on top, would you, one, try to discourage them from that? And if, two, that doesn't work, what would you suggest that they focus on most?
turns.zh: 如果有个创始人来找你说『嘿 Dan，我们是个市场，在想上面加个 SaaS 产品，你一、会劝退他吗？二、如果劝不住，你会建议他最聚焦什么？』

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I mean I think the first thing is looking at those core metrics we talked about, do they have a really liquid high performance marketplace first. That has to be the optimization function. And before you're there, I don't think you should be thinking about some of these expansion levers.
turns.zh: 我觉得第一件事是看咱们说的那些核心指标：他们是不是先有个真正流动、高性能的市场。那必须是最优化的函数。在到那之前，我觉得不该想这些扩张杠杆。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: The second would be show me the customer problem or the reason it's so hard to engage with this marketplace today that we need to build a deep set of tools or products for this customer to solve. And if both of those things are true, then I think maybe it's quite interesting. But I think more often than not, it's better to focus on the core marketplace.
turns.zh: 第二是：给我看那个客户问题、或者今天跟这市场打交道这么难、以至于我们需要给这客户建一整套深层工具或产品的理由。如果这两样都真成立，那我觉得可能挺有意思。但我觉得多数时候，聚焦核心市场更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Another common question that marketplace founders have is should I go vertical or should I go horizontal? So thinking about eBay as an example, they are very horizontal. You could buy anything you want on eBay. And then there's all these spinoffs that emerged, just classic cars, eBay for classic cars, eBay for guitars. And I'm curious if you have any advice there for either an early stage founder trying to decide should I go horizontal or vertical and/or where do you find the biggest opportunities to slice off a piece of a successful horizontal marketplace?
turns.zh: 好。市场创始人另一个常见问题：该做纵向还是横向？以 eBay 为例，它非常横向，你想买啥都能在 eBay 买。然后冒出各种衍生，比如经典车、eBay 经典车、eBay 吉他。我好奇你有没有建议——无论对早期创始人纠结横向还是纵向，还是说你在哪找到最大机会去切下成功横向市场的一块？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And in that eBay example, there are now a few quite successful examples of this like [inaudible 00:50:23] and StockX are two where they carved out the sneaker category and the key insight was you couldn't trust the inventory you were getting on eBay. So there's a lot of work you need to do to verify, and those businesses just did it much better than eBay. Broadly though, I think that we over hyped the idea of unbundling. So I think every six months I'm seeing an article where somebody wrote, "This is the unbundling of Reddit, the unbundling of LinkedIn, the unbundling of Facebook." We're going to take all those blue links that you saw on another site and they're all going to become new businesses. And very rarely that thesis plays out. I think the core logical error in the argument for unbundling is that they over focus on one type of improvement, which is user experience and they under focus on the things that make scale businesses have better economics.
turns.zh: 有，绝对。在 eBay 那个例子里，现在有俩挺成功的，比如（听不清）和 StockX——他们切出了球鞋品类，关键洞察是你在 eBay 上拿到的库存不可信。所以有很多验证的活要做，而那些生意就比 eBay 做得好得多。不过总的来说，我觉得我们高估了『拆包』这个点子。所以我差不多每六个月就看到篇文章写『这是 Reddit 的拆包、LinkedIn 的拆包、Facebook 的拆包』。我们要把你在别站看到的那些蓝链都变成新生意。而这个论点极少兑现。我觉得拆包论的逻辑错误是：他们过度聚焦一种改进，也就是用户体验，而低估了让规模生意有更好经济的东西。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And so to unpack that, if you look at UX, like if you built a LinkedIn just for construction workers or just for architects or just for investment bankers, you could definitely build some set of features that group liked better than the core LinkedIn experience. But then you have to weigh that against all of the benefits of being broader. And so the two big pieces of where you get benefits from scale are in your customer LTV and then I think the network effect you can build. So if you go back to that Thumbtack example, we had a spreadsheet which tracked hundreds of verticalized competitors where somebody would try to pick off the electricians category, the wedding category, the lessons category, and very few of them got traction for the simple reason that we could upsell customers into a thousand things.
turns.zh: 拆开说，如果你看 UX，比如你建个只给建筑工、或只给建筑师、或只给投行家的 LinkedIn，你肯定能建出让那群人比核心 LinkedIn 体验更喜欢的一些功能。但接着你得拿这个去跟『更宽』的所有好处权衡。而从规模拿到好处的两大块，是客户 LTV 和你能建的网络效应。回到 Thumbtack 例子，我们有张表追踪几百个垂直化竞争对手，有人想切电工品类、婚礼品类、课程品类，极少成气候，原因很简单：我们能向上销售客户一千样东西。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And so our customer LTV was always higher and we would always win when we were bidding against those other customers on SEM keywords that were relevant to that category. So it becomes very hard to compete if you're picking off this kind of narrow thing unless you find something which that sub-segment is itself very high frequency or very high dollar value. So Airbnb's an example. They unbundled from Craigslist because they picked off this massive high frequency, high dollar value category [inaudible 00:52:16] but there's not that many of those examples.
turns.zh: 所以我们的客户 LTV 总是更高，而且当我们在 SEM 关键词上跟那些其他客户竞标、抢那个品类相关的词时，我们总是赢。所以如果你切这种窄东西，会非常难竞争，除非你找到那个子细分本身高频或高客单价。Airbnb 就是个例子。他们从 Craigslist 拆包出来，是因为切下了这个巨大、高频、高客单价的品类（听不清），但这种例子没那么多。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And then I think the other source of benefit would be the network effect. So if you go back to LinkedIn, for example, I think actually there's an opportunity and we see some successful businesses picking off now blue collar work. So there's a company called Workrise. I think they used to be called Rigup where they're basically building like a LinkedIn but for blue collar work. And that works really well because it's a huge segment and it's somewhat self-contained.
turns.zh: 然后我觉得另一个好处来源是网络效应。回到 LinkedIn 举例，其实我觉得有个机会，我们也看到些成功的生意在切蓝领工作。有个叫 Workrise 的公司——我猜以前叫 Rigup——基本在做一个『蓝领版的 LinkedIn』。它做得很好，因为那是个巨大的细分、而且某种程度上是自成一体的。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But for most other things there's a lot of fluidity between the employers and the employees in terms of who wants to transact with one another. And so if you're an investment banker, you don't really want to be on the LinkedIn investment banker because you're probably in the future going to want some other job. So you want to be in the biggest network that's relevant to you and so this is why you can complain about LinkedIn's UI all day, but they have a very strong place in the market because of that network effect. So broadly, I think there are some pretty interesting examples, places where you can unbundle but they're rarer than people think.
turns.zh: 但对绝大多数别的东西，雇主和雇员之间在『谁想跟谁交易』上有很多流动性。所以如果你是投行家，你其实不想待在那个『LinkedIn 投行家』里，因为你将来大概率想要个别的工作。所以你想待在跟你最相关的最大网络上。这就是为什么你可以整天吐槽 LinkedIn 的 UI，但就凭那个网络效应，它在市场里有极强地位。所以总的来说，我觉得有些挺有意思的例子、有些地方你能拆包，但比人们想的稀少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is amazing. There's so much value in what you just shared. So one takeaway I have here is you have an opportunity to unbundle/split off into a vertical marketplace potentially if there's high order value and high frequency. And the third piece is there's almost a self-contained network that doesn't benefit significantly from the rest of the network. For example, I love the Rigup example, like I doubt oil rig operators are on LinkedIn and when something comes around that's like, "Oh, all my buddies are on this thing, I'm going to be on there," you don't need the rest of LinkedIn.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你刚分享的有太多价值了。所以我的一个收获是：如果有高客单价、高频，你就有机会去拆包、切出个纵向市场。第三块是：有个几乎自成一体的网络，不从其余网络显著受益。比如我超喜欢 Rigup 那个例子——我怀疑石油钻井运营商在不在 LinkedIn 上，而当出现个『嘿，我所有哥们都在这上面，我也得上』的东西，你不需要 LinkedIn 其余部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The first piece, though, is interesting. So Airbnb I wouldn't say is high frequency. I'd say it's just very large high order value. And so I wonder if you just need one or the other really in a big way. Really high order value or really high frequency?
turns.zh: 不过第一块挺有意思。我不觉得 Airbnb 是高频，我会说它只是非常大、高客单价。所以我想知道，你是不是其实只需要其中一样特别强就行——要么极高客单价，要么极高频？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: This is a good point. Probably what you're solving for is customer LTV and you can get that in multiple places. There's not that many things which are both high frequency and high dollar value so you can do both. I do think if you go to a place that is low frequency, it comes with all kinds of new challenges because, without frequency, customers forget about you. And so what is the hook to get them to come back? Do you have to reacquire traffic? It creates a whole other set of problems. But if you can get it right like in the Airbnb case, it can work really well.
turns.zh: 好点。你大概在求解的是客户 LTV，而你可以在多处拿到它。又高频又高客单价的东西没那么多，所以你可以两者都要。但我觉得如果你去一个低频的地方，它会带来各种新挑战，因为没有频率，客户就把你忘了。那把他们拉回来的钩子是什么？你得重新获客吗？这造出一整套别的问题。但如果你能像 Airbnb 那样做对，它会非常好使。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, Thumbtack is a classic example of how often you need a plumber. And even with the thousands of services that you all had, from what I understand, it's still a struggle to get people to come back often. And remember Thumbtack when they had, "Oh, they have an electrician. Oh yeah, Thumbtack."
turns.zh: 对，Thumbtack 就是个经典例子——你得多久叫一次水管工。即便你们有上千种服务，据我所知，让人常回来仍是挣扎。还记得 Thumbtack 当时『哦他们有个电工。哦对，Thumbtack。』

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: That's right. Initially, it was very difficult. I mean the average person hires eight or ten new professionals a year, the average homeowner. And so that's decently high frequency, but it's not food delivery or a ride sharing or something like that.
turns.zh: 对。一开始非常难。我是说普通房主一年雇八到十个新专业人士。所以频率还算可以，但远不是外卖或打车那种。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to Faire, so Faire is one of the maybe few really successful B2B marketplaces and it's always felt like there's this gap in B2B marketplaces. You always feel like there should be many more. Like why are there so many consumer marketplaces but so few B2B, and I'm curious what's your take there. Do you think there's a rising trend to B2B marketplaces? Do you think this is always going to be a smaller collection? What's your feeling?
turns.zh: 回到 Faire。Faire 大概是少数真正成功的 B2B 市场之一，而且一直让人感觉 B2B 市场有个缺口。你总觉得应该有更多才对。为什么消费类市场那么多、B2B 却这么少？我好奇你的看法。你觉得 B2B 市场有大趋势在起吗？还是觉得这永远会是个更小的集合？你什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: So I do think we'll see more of them. Part of the reason we've seen fewer is there are fewer potential founders who understand B2B problems because most of them are consumers and so the consumer use cases are more obvious. So if you take Faire, for example, when I met the founders, which is probably five years ago now, I immediately understood what they were talking about, but only because I had run an e-commerce business in the past and I had the experience of dealing with a hundred suppliers and line sheets and PDFs going back and forth and pricing not being right and just how painful it is to be a retail buyer. And they had a solution which was much better and that clicked.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得我们会看到更多。我们见得少的部分原因，是懂 B2B 问题的潜在创始人更少，因为他们大多是从消费者视角，所以消费类用例更明显。拿 Faire 说，我大概五年前见创始人，我立刻就懂他们在说啥，但只因为以前我运营过一个电商生意，有过跟上百个供应商、报价单、来回 PDF、价格不对、以及当零售买手有多痛苦的体验。而他们有个好得多的方案，一下就通了。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But had I had the same conversation five or 10 years ago with the team at Convoy like I don't know anything about trucking, I probably wouldn't have understood why that business was going to work. And so I think there's partly that. Just the discovery process takes longer for that reason. But I think the reason we won't see a huge explosion in this area is that B2B also comes with something else, which is much lower fragmentation in many cases and you need fragmentation for a good marketplace. The more concentrated either side of your market is, the more leverage they have, the less likely they are to need you and the less likely they are to be willing to pay a high commission.
turns.zh: 但如果五年或十年前我跟 Convoy 那团队聊——我对卡车运输一窍不通——我大概不会懂那生意为什么能成。所以我觉得有一部分就是这个。就因为这个，发现过程要更长。但我觉得我们不会在这领域看到大爆发的原因是：B2B 还带来另一件事——很多情况下碎片化低得多，而好市场需要碎片化。你市场任一侧越集中，他们杠杆越大、越不需要你、越不愿付高佣金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You made that point to me once when we were talking about marketplaces years ago, and that's so stuck with me that when evaluating marketplaces in B2B especially, usually the reason it's not going to work is just it's not fragmented enough. And just to double click there, can you explain what that means? What does fragmentation mean in a marketplace context? And then are there any examples of really low fragmentation of this will never work as a marketplace? And then here it's really high and this is why it's working?
turns.zh: 你几年前跟我说市场时点了这点，我印象极深：评估 B2B 市场尤其时，它不成的原因通常就是『不够碎片化』。就顺着这点展开，你能解释下这是什么意思吗？市场语境下的碎片化是什么？有没有什么『碎片化极低、这辈子成不了市场』的例子？以及什么『碎片化极高、所以它能成』？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Fragmentation is basically just a measure of how many total businesses are there in the space relative to the transaction volume in that space. And if you took the top 5% of suppliers in the space, what percentage of the total volume are they doing? And the higher that percentage is, the less fragmented you are. The challenge that creates for a marketplace is if there's 10 companies in a space that are doing 80% of the volume, it's very important for me to have a relationship with those 10 companies. But those 10 companies are also big enough to have their own sales teams, have their own internal operations. They just need less from a marketplace and, as a result, they're going to be willing to pay less. And you're also probably going to see many more problems with disintermediation, which is when the supplier and the customer go around the marketplace because they can just transact themselves.
turns.zh: 碎片化基本就是：这个领域里总共有多少企业，相对这个领域的总交易量。如果取这个领域前 5% 的供给方，他们占了总交易量的百分之多少？那个百分比越高，你越不碎片化。它给市场造的难题是：如果一个领域 10 家公司做了 80% 的量，那我跟这 10 家搞好关系就极其重要。但这 10 家也大到有自己的销售团队、自己的内部运营。他们从市场那需要得更少，结果就是他们愿意付得更少。而且你大概会看到多得多的『去中介化』问题——就是供给方和客户绕过市场直接交易，因为他们自己就能成交。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: One principle to use here is how many total dollars are attached to each transaction in the marketplace. When it goes above a certain amount, it becomes much more attractive to figure out how to go around the marketplace. With ride sharing, for example, the absolute dollars of commission on a ride is $2 or $3. Is it worth it for the driver to figure out how to call the passenger two minutes in advance, go around Uber and pick them up? Maybe. You probably see some of that happening, but usually not.
turns.zh: 这里能用的一条原则是：市场里每笔交易挂的总金额有多大。当它超过某个数，去想怎么绕过市场就变得诱人多得多。拿打车说，一趟的佣金钱绝对就 2 块或 3 块。司机值得去想怎么提前两分钟打电话给乘客、绕过 Uber 去接他吗？也许。你大概会看到一些这种事，但通常不会。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But now take there's a bunch of people in the kind of material space within B2B marketplaces, you have manufacturers of say beauty products who need to source aerosol cans and all the inputs into making beauty products. There's not that many of these big suppliers and each of their transactions may be tens of thousands of dollars, hundreds of thousands of dollars, millions of dollars. The commission you would charge on that order is too high because a supplier would rather just pick up the phone and call this person and save those tens of thousands of dollars. And so you just run into these kind of fundamental problems where a marketplace doesn't work anymore.
turns.zh: 但再看 B2B 市场里『原材料』那块，你有比如美妆产品制造商，需要采购气雾罐和做美妆的所有原料。这种大供应商没多少，而他们每笔交易可能是几万、几十万、上百万美元。你在这单上收的佣金会太高，因为供应商宁愿直接打电话给那人、省下那几万块。于是你就撞上这种根本问题：市场不再管用了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. Basically, how much value are you bringing to this market? And if it's not enough where you can charge anything meaningful to run a business is just not going to work. And so that's a really good way of framing it.
turns.zh: 说得通。本质就是：你给这市场带来多少价值？如果少到收不出什么有意义、能养起生意的费用，那就根本不成。所以这是个很好的框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question around marketplaces and, broadly, and I'll let you go. You've spent a lot of time on marketplaces. You've seen their evolution. You've worked on this maybe for the past decade. Where do you see the future of marketplaces going?
turns.zh: 关于市场的最后一个问题，广义上，然后就放你走。你在市场花了大量时间，见过它们的演化，大概过去十年都在做。你看市场的未来往哪走？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: I actually wrote a blog post on this where we charted the commission that a marketplace charges and the year they were founded. And if you put those on the x and y axis, there's this very clear up into the right trend. Newer marketplaces are charging higher commissions and they're doing more work to justify those commissions. So broadly the evolution looks like kind of Marketplace 1.0, which is all they're doing is aggregating demand. So that's Zillow and Home Advisor. They're basically like lead gen and their commission rate is often pretty low. It's like 5%, maybe 10%.
turns.zh: 其实我写了篇博客聊这个，我们把市场收的佣金和它成立的年份画在一起。把这两个放 xy 轴，有个非常清楚的向右上走的趋势。 newer 市场收更高佣金，而且它们做更多活来justify那些佣金。所以广义的演化像是：市场 1.0，只做聚合需求。就是 Zillow 和 Home Advisor。基本像线索生成，佣金率常很低，5%、最多 10%。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Then you have a managed marketplace like Airbnb or Etsy, which did something really fundamental on top of that, which is generated trust. So they deadhead supply ... You could probably tell me more about what Airbnb did in this space, but they made it a safe transaction and there's a lot of work it takes to make that transaction trustworthy and safe and so they charge a higher commission as a result.
turns.zh: 然后你有像 Airbnb 或 Etsy 这种受管理的市场，在之上做了件根本的事——建立信任。所以他们筛掉差供给……这领域 Airbnb 做了啥你大概能讲更多，但他们让交易变得安全，而让交易可信又安全要做大量工作，所以作为结果他们收更高佣金。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: There's then one click beyond that which, for lack of a better term, you could call it a heavily managed marketplace, but now they're typically doing some work in the value chain, which is distinct from just aggregating demand. So DoorDash and Instacart own logistics. They took over logistics and, as a result, DoorDash did a much better job than the previous model of Seamless of being able to bring on a lot more restaurants and make it much more reliable for the customer. As a result, they could charge more to the restaurant. Similarly, Faire, we actually underwrite the transaction. We take the risk. If that transaction falls through or the retailer defaults, Faire eats that. And so we are playing a much more fundamental place in that transaction.
turns.zh: 再往外一步，姑且叫『重管理市场』，现在他们通常在价值链里做点事，跟单纯聚合需求不同。所以 DoorDash 和 Instacart 拥有物流。他们接管了物流，结果 DoorDash 比之前的 Seamless 模型做得好得多——能带更多餐厅进来、让客户体验可靠得多。所以作为结果，他们能向餐厅收更多。类似的，Faire 我们其实是给交易做授信、我们担风险。如果交易黄了或零售商违约，Faire 吃下。所以我们在那笔交易里处在一个根本得多的位置。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: But as you play this out, what happens at the end of this continuum? Ultimately, you're charging a hundred percent commission and you're not a marketplace anymore. So I think, as we think about the future of marketplaces, one important question is which marketplaces are going to tend towards evolving out of the marketplace model altogether and which will stay in marketplace mode in equilibrium? And you see these examples already like people talk about Opendoor as a marketplace, but it's not. It's an e-commerce website which has the highest price points you can imagine because you're buying houses, but there's no supplier on the other side. They've already bought the house so it's just e-commerce. And I think many marketplaces will go that way. And I think the variable to me that matters in deciding which case you're going to have, whether they consolidate or not, is how much creativity there is in the space. So how much do you need the supplier to be coming up with interesting new things for your customers to buy.
turns.zh: 但你把这推到底，这连续体的尽头发生什么？最终你收百分之百佣金，你就不再是市场了。所以我觉得，当我们想市场的未来，一个重要问题是：哪些市场会趋向于彻底演化出市场模型、哪些会停在市场模式达到均衡？你现在已经看到这种例子，比如人们说 Opendoor 是个市场，但它不是。它是个电商网站，价格点是你能想象的最高，因为你在买房，但另一侧没有供给方。他们已经把房买了，所以就是电商。我觉得很多市场会走那条路。而决定你属于哪种情况——它们会不会整合——的变量，是这领域有多少创造性。也就是客户要买的有趣新东西，有多需要供给方来想出来。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: What the customer cares about is actually commoditization. They want the same experience every time. Then you're ultimately going to evolve away from marketplaces I think. With ride sharing, basically what I want is a clean car that shows up on time and gets me there every time. So as soon as autonomous vehicles arrive, we're going to fully consolidate that industry and it's not going to be marketplace model any more. On the other end, you have Etsy and Amazon. I think Faire's in this bucket. Steam, the video game marketplace, is in this bucket where the thing you care about is suppliers bringing you amazing creative new things. And that's something that big companies are really bad at doing. So they need the marketplace suppliers to supply this. And so I think those businesses stay in marketplace mode longer term.
turns.zh: 客户在乎的其实是商品化。他们每次都想要同样的体验。那最终你会演化离开市场，我觉得。拿打车，我基本就想要一辆干净的车、准时到、每次都把我送到。所以自动驾驶一来，我们就会彻底整合那个行业，它不再是市场模型。另一头，你有 Etsy 和亚马逊。我觉得 Faire 在这桶里。Steam、那个游戏市场，也在这桶里——你在乎的是供给方给你带来惊艳的创意新东西。而那是大公司极不擅长的。所以他们需要市场供给方来供这个。所以我觉得那些生意长期停在市场模式。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: And then the middle, I don't exactly know how to call what happens in food delivery. You do want some standardization elements, but you also want the local restaurants and so does DoorDash win or the Cloud Kitchen model win? I think it's a little bit harder to understand, but I do think that's kind of the variable that's determining where the future of marketplaces are going.
turns.zh: 中间那块，我不太确定外卖到底算什么。你确实想要些标准化元素，但也想要本地餐厅，所以到底是 DoorDash 赢、还是 Cloud Kitchen 模型赢？我觉得有点更难懂，但我觉得那就是决定市场未来走向的变量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting to think about this event horizon for when a marketplace is no longer a marketplace. Is a simple way to think about that being when you own the supply, you're no longer a marketplace. When you don't own the supply, you are. Is that how you think about that?
turns.zh: 有意思，去想『市场不再是市场』的那个事件视界。一个简单想法是不是：当你拥有供给，你就不再是市场；当你不拥有供给，你就是。你是这么想的吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, that's a good mental [inaudible 01:02:37]. Perhaps another way to say owning a supply is when there's no longer a direct transaction between supply and demand. That's what Opendoor took out, for example. You're not transacting with the home seller. You're transacting with Open Door and so that's, in my mind, no longer a marketplace because you also eliminate some of the marketplace mechanics we were talking about a bit.
turns.zh: 对，那是个好心智……（听不清）。也许说『拥有供给』的另一种方式是：当供给和需求之间不再有直接交易。那就是 Opendoor 去掉的东西。你不是跟卖房者交易，你是跟 Opendoor 交易，所以在我的心智里，那不再是市场，因为你也去掉了咱们聊过的某些市场机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Dan, this has been incredible. I feel like we've achieved our goal of getting really deep into the weeds on growth models and marketplaces. Two final questions for you.
turns.zh: 好。Dan，这太了不起了。我觉得我们达成了目标——在增长模型和市场这两块真的钻到了杂草深处。最后两个问题给你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where can folks find you online if they want to learn more, reach out and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 大家想多学、想联系的话，网上去哪找你？听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Yeah, so I'm on Twitter at Dan Hockenmaier and then LinkedIn. People should feel free to reach out. I think the most useful thing is we're always growing our team at Faire. And so for folks who are interested in this space, I would love to connect with them.
turns.zh: 我在 Twitter 上是 Dan Hockenmaier，还有 LinkedIn。大家随时可以联系。最有用的其实是：我们在 Faire 一直在扩团队。所以对这领域感兴趣的人，我很乐意跟他们连接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where do they go to learn more and apply for Faire?
turns.zh: 他们去哪多了解、以及申请 Faire？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Just faire.com or faire.com/careers.
turns.zh: 就 faire.com，或 faire.com/careers。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's Faire with an "e" at the end?
turns.zh: 是结尾带个『e』的 Faire 吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: That's correct, yes.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. All right, Dan, thank you for being here.
turns.zh: 好。行，Dan，谢谢你来。

turns.speaker: Dan Hockenmaier
turns.en: Thank you so much for the time.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你抽出时间。

turns.en: Thank you so much for listening.
